"No Tax on Overtime" and Your 2026 W-2s: What Employers Must Report by February 1

FLAT Staffing · December 7, 2026 · 5 min read

For employers with a lot of hourly overtime, and that describes most distribution centers, auction operations and dealership service departments in peak, year-end payroll has a new step this time. Starting with 2026 wages, the IRS requires employers to report "qualified overtime compensation" separately on Form W-2 so employees can claim the new federal overtime deduction.

If your payroll provider has not talked with you about it yet, now is the time. Here is what the rule requires and what to check before your final payroll of the year.

The deduction in brief

The federal tax law enacted in 2025 created a deduction for qualified overtime compensation. According to the IRS:

  • It is effective for tax years 2025 through 2028.
  • Eligible workers can deduct up to $12,500 per return, or $25,000 on a joint return.
  • The deduction phases out for modified adjusted gross income above $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers).
  • It is available whether or not the worker itemizes.

This is an income tax deduction the employee claims on their return. It does not change payroll taxes. The IRS says overtime is still subject to Social Security and Medicare tax for both employer and employee, and to income tax withholding.

What counts as "qualified overtime"

This is where precision matters. The IRS defines qualified overtime compensation as the premium portion of overtime that the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) requires, the "half" in time and a half.

Under the general method in the IRS FAQs, it equals hours over 40 in a workweek, times one-half, times the employee's FLSA regular rate.

Example: an employee whose regular rate is $20 works 50 hours. They are paid $30 an hour for 10 overtime hours, or $300. The qualified overtime is only the premium: 10 x $10 = $100.

The IRS lists several things that do not qualify:

  • Overtime not required by the FLSA, including premiums paid only because of state law, a union contract or your own policy. If you pay double time, only the FLSA-required portion counts.
  • Pay to FLSA-exempt employees, such as salaried executive, administrative and professional staff.
  • Pay to certain 20 percent owners who actively manage the business.

Why your regular rate matters here

Because qualified overtime is based on the regular rate, anything that belongs in the regular rate affects the number you report. Nondiscretionary bonuses, such as peak attendance or production incentives, must be included in the regular rate under DOL rules. If your payroll system calculates overtime on base pay alone, both the overtime you paid and the amount you report on the W-2 may be wrong. We covered how bonuses change the regular rate in our post on peak-season incentives.

What changes on the 2026 Form W-2

According to the IRS's 2026 instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3:

  • Box 12, code TT is new and reports the total amount of qualified overtime compensation.
  • Report the full amount paid, even if it exceeds the employee's deduction limit. The IRS FAQs give the example of $30,000 paid being reported in full.
  • For tips, there is a separate new box 12, code TP, and box 14b for Treasury tipped occupation codes. Most of the industries we work with will not use these.

For 2025, the IRS did not require separate reporting and offered transition relief. For 2026 and later, separate reporting is required.

In rare cases where a worker is an FLSA employee but an independent contractor for tax purposes, the amount goes on Form 1099-NEC box 1d or 1099-MISC box 14 instead.

Key deadlines and other 2026 changes

  • W-2 deadline: The IRS instructions say 2026 Forms W-2 are due to the Social Security Administration and to employees by February 1, 2027.
  • 1099-NEC threshold: For payments after 2025, the reporting threshold rose from $600 to $2,000.
  • Penalties: The IRS says penalty amounts for late or incorrect information returns increased for returns due after December 31, 2026.
  • Corrections: If you find an error after filing, the IRS FAQs say to file a Form W-2c and furnish it to the employee as soon as possible.
  • Withholding: Employers do not reduce income tax withholding for this deduction unless the employee submits an updated Form W-4.

Steps to take before your last 2026 payroll

  1. Confirm your payroll system tracks the FLSA premium separately for each non-exempt employee, and that it will populate box 12, code TT.
  2. Check your regular rate calculation, especially if you paid peak bonuses, shift differentials or other incentives.
  3. Separate FLSA overtime from extra overtime. If you pay daily overtime or double time by policy, make sure only the FLSA-required premium is reported.
  4. Review exempt classifications so salaried exempt staff are not reported.
  5. Prepare employees for questions. Some will expect their whole overtime check to be tax-free. A short explanation of what the W-2 shows, and a referral to a tax professional, can head off frustration in February.

If you use temporary workers

For temps placed through a staffing agency, the agency is the employer of record and issues the W-2, including box 12, code TT. Your role is to make sure hours are approved accurately and that any incentives you funded were communicated to the agency so they are in the regular rate.

This article is general information, not tax or legal advice. Rules may continue to be updated, so confirm details with your payroll provider, CPA or the IRS.

The bottom line

For 2026, qualified overtime goes in box 12, code TT on Form W-2, and it is only the FLSA-required premium based on the regular rate. Get your payroll setup right in December, and your W-2s will be ready by February 1.

Your Arizona Unemployment Tax Rate: How It's Set and How Seasonal Layoffs Affect It

FLAT Staffing · December 4, 2026 · 5 min read

Most employers look at their unemployment insurance rate once a year, when the notice arrives, and then forget about it. But for operations with big seasonal swings, such as distribution centers that ramp up for peak or dealerships that staff up for year-end events, the way you hire and release people affects that rate for years.

Here is how Arizona's system works, what drives your rate up or down and what to do before the new rate year begins.

The basics

Arizona employers pay state unemployment insurance (UI) tax to the Arizona Department of Economic Security (DES). A few key figures:

  • Taxable wage base: UI tax applies to the first $8,000 paid to each employee in a calendar year, under A.R.S. 23-622.
  • New employer rate: New employers are assigned 2.0 percent for at least two calendar years, according to DES.
  • 2026 rates: Based on the DES rate chart for 2026, rates ranged from 0.03 percent to 4.18 percent for employers with a positive reserve ratio and from 4.41 percent to 8.36 percent for employers with a negative ratio.

There is also the federal unemployment tax (FUTA). Per an Arizona Senate research brief, the FUTA rate is 6.0 percent on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, with a credit of up to 5.4 percent for employers who pay state taxes on time, for a typical net rate of 0.6 percent.

Because the $8,000 state wage base is low, a high-turnover operation pays UI tax on a larger share of its total payroll. Ten people who each work two months can generate more taxable wages than two people who work the full year.

How your rate is calculated

DES uses what it calls a reserve ratio system:

  1. Your reserve balance is the UI taxes you have paid in, minus the unemployment benefits charged to your account.
  2. That balance is divided by your average annual taxable payroll over up to three fiscal years.
  3. The resulting ratio, positive or negative, places you in a rate group on the DES tax rate chart.

A higher ratio means a lower rate. Benefit charges reduce your reserve, so when former employees collect unemployment based on wages you paid, your ratio falls and your future rate can rise. DES also notes that statewide conditions matter: high unemployment can push rates up across the board, and low unemployment can bring them down.

Each year, DES sends a Determination of Unemployment Tax Rate notice showing your rate and the factors behind it, along with how to appeal if you think it is wrong.

Why seasonal layoffs push your rate up

When you hire directly for peak and release those workers in January, some of them may file for unemployment. If their claims are based on wages you paid, the benefits can be charged to your account. Repeat that every year and your reserve ratio can drift downward, moving you into a higher rate group.

A few habits help:

  • Plan headcount carefully. Hiring more people than you need and releasing them after a few weeks increases potential claims.
  • Respond to claim notices on time and with accurate separation information, so DES has what it needs to decide each claim correctly.
  • Track your rate over several years, not just one. A creeping rate is a signal to look at turnover and seasonal hiring practices.

The voluntary payment option

Arizona allows employers to make a voluntary contribution to their UI account to raise their reserve ratio and potentially drop into a lower rate group. According to DES:

  • The payment must be made by February 28 to lower your rate for that calendar year.
  • Your annual rate notice explains how to calculate the amount needed.
  • Compare the payment to the tax savings before deciding. It only makes sense if the savings exceed the payment.

DES recommends paying by check, noting the purpose and sending it to the UI Tax Experience Rating Unit. Instructions are on the back of the rate notice. Mark your calendar for when the notice arrives so you have time to run the numbers.

Where temporary staffing fits

When your seasonal workers come through a staffing agency, the agency is the employer of record. It pays the wages, pays the UI tax on those wages and handles unemployment claims from those workers. Their separations do not run through your UI account.

That is one reason many employers keep a stable core of direct employees and use temporary staffing for the peaks. Your own account reflects your steady workforce, while the swings are handled by the agency. The cost of that coverage is built into the bill rate, so compare it honestly against your own fully loaded cost, including UI, when you plan.

If you convert a temp to your direct payroll, that person becomes your employee, and future UI tax and any benefit charges based on your wages follow you from that point.

A year-end UI checklist

  1. Watch for your rate notice and check the figures against your records.
  2. Calculate whether a voluntary payment pays off before February 28.
  3. Update your payroll system with the new rate before the first 2027 payroll.
  4. Review last year's claims and how quickly your team responded to DES notices.
  5. Plan 2027 seasonal hiring with UI costs in mind: direct hires, temps or a mix.

This article is general information, not tax or legal advice. Confirm your rate, payment options and obligations with Arizona DES or your payroll provider.

The bottom line

Your Arizona UI rate reflects how you hire and release people. Seasonal swings on your own payroll can raise it over time. Review your notice, consider a voluntary payment by February 28 and think about which part of your workforce belongs on your payroll and which belongs with a staffing partner.

If you want to model direct hire against temporary staffing for your 2027 peaks, talk with our team or call 602-730-3312.

OSHA 300 Logs and Temp Workers: Who Records the Injury, and What's Due in 2027

FLAT Staffing · December 2, 2026 · 5 min read

December is when safety managers start thinking about the OSHA 300 log. The year's records need to be reviewed and closed out, a summary has to go up on the wall by February 1, and many warehouse and distribution employers have to submit data to OSHA electronically by March 2.

There is one question that comes up every year at sites that use temporary labor: when a temp gets hurt, whose log does it go on? The answer surprises a lot of host employers.

The rule: whoever supervises day to day records it

OSHA's recordkeeping regulation, 29 CFR 1904.31, says you must record injuries and illnesses of employees on your payroll and of workers who are not on your payroll if you supervise them on a day-to-day basis. It specifically covers workers provided by a temporary staffing service.

In other words, if your leads direct the temp's daily work, the injury goes on your OSHA 300 log, even though the staffing agency pays the worker and carries the workers' comp policy.

OSHA's interpretation letters add a few useful details:

  • Day-to-day supervision means directing the details, means, methods and processes of the work, not just telling the agency what output you need.
  • Each case is recorded only once. The staffing agency does not also record a case that goes on the host's log. The two companies should coordinate.
  • The facts on the floor control, not the contract. A clause saying "the agency handles all recordkeeping" does not change who supervises the work.
  • In one OSHA letter, an agency handled HR tasks like leave, benefits, drug screening and discipline, and even had on-site staff. OSHA said that was not day-to-day supervision. The host assigned the daily tasks, so the host had to record the injuries.

This is different from workers' compensation, where the agency as employer of record typically carries the coverage and handles the claim. Recordkeeping and comp follow different rules.

What makes a case recordable

Not every scrape goes on the log. According to OSHA, a work-related injury or illness is recordable if it results in:

  • Death
  • Days away from work
  • Restricted work or transfer to another job
  • Medical treatment beyond first aid
  • Loss of consciousness
  • A significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional

Covered employers keep the OSHA 300 Log, the 301 Incident Reports and the 300A Annual Summary, and retain them for five years. Some smaller employers and certain low-hazard industries are partially exempt from routine recordkeeping; check OSHA's criteria if you are unsure.

Year-end steps and deadlines

Review and certify the 300A

Under 29 CFR 1904.32, after the year ends you must review the log for accuracy, fix errors and complete the Form 300A summary, including the average number of employees and total hours worked. A company executive must certify it: an owner, a corporate officer, the highest-ranking official at the establishment or that person's immediate supervisor.

If you supervised temps day to day and recorded their injuries, think about how their hours fit into your totals so the summary is consistent with the log. Ask your staffing partner for hours worked at your site; they have them on payroll.

Post it from February 1 to April 30

The certified 300A must be posted where employee notices are usually posted, from February 1 through April 30. OSHA says this applies even if you had no recordable cases; you post a summary with zeros.

Submit electronically by March 2

Under 29 CFR 1904.41, certain establishments must submit injury data to OSHA through its Injury Tracking Application by March 2 of the following year:

  • Establishments with 250 or more employees that must keep records submit the 300A.
  • Establishments with 20 to 249 employees in designated industries submit the 300A. OSHA's list includes warehousing and storage (NAICS 4931) and wholesale trade (NAICS 42).
  • Establishments with 100 or more employees in a separate list of designated industries must also submit 300 and 301 data.

OSHA notes that part-time, seasonal and temporary workers count toward these employee totals. A distribution center that ran a large peak crew in 2026 could cross a threshold it doesn't usually reach. Check OSHA's coverage tool if you're unsure.

Report severe injuries right away

Separately from the log, serious events have to be reported quickly. ADOSH, Arizona's state OSHA program, requires employers to report work-related fatalities within 8 hours and in-patient hospitalizations, amputations and eye losses within 24 hours. ADOSH's reporting line is (602) 542-5795.

Coordinate with your staffing partner

  1. Agree on the reporting path. Temps should report injuries to their site lead and to the agency right away.
  2. Share incident information quickly so whoever records the case has what they need within OSHA's timeframes.
  3. Confirm whose log it goes on, based on who actually directs the work.
  4. Get temp hours by site at year end for your 300A totals.
  5. Review the cases together. Patterns in temp injuries often point to training or onboarding gaps you can fix before next peak.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Consult your safety professional or counsel about your specific recordkeeping obligations.

The bottom line

If your supervisors direct a temp's daily work, that temp's recordable injuries belong on your OSHA 300 log. Close out the year carefully, certify and post the 300A by February 1, submit by March 2 if you're covered and coordinate with your agency so every case is recorded once, correctly.

Hiring Teens for Winter Break: What 16- and 17-Year-Olds Can and Can't Do in Warehouses and Lots

FLAT Staffing · November 30, 2026 · 5 min read

When schools let out for winter break, a lot of teenagers want work, and a lot of employers still need hands for holiday peak and post-holiday returns. Hiring a 16- or 17-year-old for a few weeks can be a good fit for both. But the rules for minors are stricter than many supervisors expect, and some of the most common tasks in warehouses and on car lots are off-limits until 18.

Child labor violations can bring civil money penalties, and DOL says those can be higher when a violation contributes to a minor's injury and doubled for willful or repeated violations. Here is what to know before you put a teenager on the schedule.

Federal and Arizona rules both apply

Both the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and Arizona law regulate youth employment. The Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA) notes that when both apply, the more restrictive requirement controls.

Hours: 16 and 17 vs. 14 and 15

Under federal law, 16- and 17-year-olds have no limits on hours or times of day. They can work full shifts during winter break in any job that is not declared hazardous. Confirm with the ICA whether any Arizona-specific rules apply to your situation.

Younger teens are a different story. Under DOL rules, 14- and 15-year-olds may work only outside school hours, no more than 3 hours on a school day, 18 hours in a school week, 8 hours on a non-school day and 40 hours in a non-school week, and generally only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. outside the summer. More importantly for our industries, the ICA lists warehousing among occupations prohibited for workers 15 and under. In practice, warehouse and lot employers should plan on hiring 16 and older.

Jobs that are off-limits until 18

Federal Hazardous Occupations Orders (HOs) bar workers under 18 from certain jobs no matter how many hours they work. The ones that matter most for warehouses, dealerships and auctions:

Forklifts and other lifting equipment (HO 7)

Workers under 18 may not operate, ride on or assist with most power-driven hoisting equipment. According to DOL, that includes forklifts, skid-steers, manlifts, scissor lifts and cranes. A 17-year-old can pick, pack and stage freight by hand, but should not be on a forklift, order picker or reach truck, even "just to move one pallet."

DOL does carve out electric or pneumatic lifts used to raise cars in garages and service stations, which is relevant for some dealership service departments. Read the order carefully before relying on it.

Balers and compactors (HO 12)

Minors may not operate balers or compactors. Under specific conditions, 16- and 17-year-olds may load, but not operate or unload, certain scrap paper balers and paper box compactors. In a distribution center with cardboard balers on every dock, set a clear rule that minors stay away from them.

Power saws (HO 14)

Operating or helping with power-driven circular, band, chain and reciprocating saws is prohibited for minors.

Driving (HO 2)

This is the big one for auction and dealership employers. Under federal law:

  • 16-year-olds may not drive on public roads as part of their job.
  • 17-year-olds may drive only in narrow circumstances. Per DOL Fact Sheet #34, the driving must be occasional and incidental (no more than one-third of the workday and 20 percent of the workweek), in daylight, in a car or small truck rated at 6,000 pounds or less, with seat belts, within 30 miles of the workplace, by a teen who has a valid license, completed driver education and had no moving violations at hire.
  • Even then, 17-year-olds may not tow vehicles, make urgent time-sensitive deliveries, do route deliveries or carry more than three passengers.

Arizona adds its own limits on young drivers. The ICA's guidance describes total driving time limits and a cap on daily driving distance for 16- and 17-year-olds, and also notes the federal restriction. Because the more restrictive rule controls, most dealership and auction employers simply keep minors out of driving roles.

The DOL fact sheet focuses on public roads. If you are thinking about having a minor move cars on a private lot, get advice first.

Practical guidelines for winter-break hires

  1. Verify age before the first shift. Keep proof of age in the file.
  2. Write down the prohibited tasks for each minor's role and give a copy to the supervisor.
  3. Badge or flag minors so leads know at a glance who cannot operate equipment.
  4. Train in plain language. New, young workers need clear instruction on what they can and cannot touch.
  5. Assign appropriate work. Hand picking, packing, labeling, cleaning, staging and returns processing are often good fits, as long as no prohibited equipment is involved.
  6. Watch for "helping out." Most child labor violations on the floor happen when a busy lead asks a minor to jump on equipment for a minute.

Temps under 18

Many staffing agencies set their own minimum ages for certain assignments, often 18 for any role involving equipment or driving. If you want to include 16- or 17-year-olds in a seasonal crew, discuss it with your agency first so both sides understand which tasks are allowed.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Youth employment rules have many details and exceptions. Confirm your specific obligations with the ICA, DOL or employment counsel.

The bottom line

Teens on winter break can help cover peak and returns, but forklifts, balers, power saws and most driving are off-limits until 18. Hire 16 and older for warehouse work, define the allowed tasks in writing and make sure every supervisor knows the rules.

If you need seasonal help that can run equipment and drive, talk with our team or call 602-730-3312.

Final Paychecks After Peak: Arizona's Rules When Seasonal Work Ends

FLAT Staffing · November 27, 2026 · 4 min read

The day after Thanksgiving is the start of the busiest stretch of the year for many distribution centers. It is also a good time to plan the other end of peak: what happens when volume drops and seasonal workers leave in late December and January.

Arizona has specific rules about when final wages are due, and the deadline depends on whether the employee was let go or quit. Getting it wrong is not just a paperwork issue. Arizona law allows employees to recover up to three times unpaid wages in some cases. Here is what operations and HR leaders should know before the wind-down.

The two deadlines

Arizona's final pay rule is A.R.S. 23-353.

When you discharge an employee (including ending employment because seasonal work is over), wages due must be paid within seven working days or by the end of the next regular pay period, whichever is sooner.

When an employee quits, wages are due no later than the regular payday for the pay period in which the employee left. The employee can ask to receive the payment by mail.

For a seasonal layoff, the first rule usually applies. If you are on a biweekly payroll and the next payday is ten working days away, the seven-working-day deadline comes first, which can mean an off-cycle check.

How final pay must be delivered

The statute requires payment in a form that can be cashed immediately at face value, or by deposit into a financial institution the employee has chosen. Plan how you will deliver final checks to people who will not be returning to the site, and keep addresses and direct deposit information current through peak.

What happens if pay is late

Two points worth knowing:

  • Treble damages. Under A.R.S. 23-355, an employee who sues over wages the employer failed to pay may recover up to three times the unpaid amount.
  • State wage claims. The Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA) accepts unpaid wage claims of up to $12,000, filed within one year of when the claim accrued. Larger amounts go to the U.S. Department of Labor or to court. The ICA form notes that overtime, minimum wage, earned paid sick time and retaliation claims are handled separately.

Paid sick time at separation

Arizona's earned paid sick time law affects the wind-down in two ways, according to the ICA's FAQs:

  • No payout is required. Employers do not have to pay out unused earned paid sick time at separation, though they may choose to.
  • Rehire within nine months. If you rehire an employee within nine months of separation, previously accrued, unused sick time generally must be reinstated, and the employee can use and accrue time right away. The ICA has said it will not enforce reinstatement against an employer that paid out the unused time at separation, if the employee accepted that payment.

That nine-month window matters for seasonal operations. Many of the people you release in January may be exactly the people you want back for next peak, or even for spring returns. Track separation dates and sick time balances so rehires are handled correctly.

Plan the wind-down in steps

Here is the approach we recommend:

  1. Set your ramp-down calendar now. Decide which weeks you expect volume to drop and how many people you will release each week.
  2. Map final pay deadlines to your payroll calendar. For each release date, figure out whether you will hit the seven-working-day deadline on your regular payday or need an off-cycle run.
  3. Collect final timecards promptly. Make sure supervisors approve the last week's hours quickly, including any missed punches.
  4. Include everything owed. Final wages include regular pay, overtime and any earned bonuses. If you promised an end-of-peak attendance bonus, pay it if earned, and remember it affects the regular rate for overtime.
  5. Handle equipment returns carefully. Arizona has specific rules about wage deductions. Talk to payroll or counsel before deducting for unreturned badges, scanners or uniforms.
  6. Identify your keepers. Flag top performers for rehire, conversion or next season. Tell them you want them back.
  7. Record separation reasons accurately. Records matter for unemployment claims and for future rehire decisions.

How this works with temporary workers

When your seasonal labor comes through a staffing agency, the agency is the employer of record and handles final pay, sick time balances and unemployment paperwork. Ending an assignment on your site does not always end the worker's employment with the agency, which may place them elsewhere.

Your part is simpler but still important:

  • Give your agency advance notice of release dates so it can plan reassignments and payroll.
  • Approve final hours quickly so the agency can meet its own deadlines.
  • Tell the agency who you would like back for future peaks or for conversion to direct hire.

This is one of the practical advantages of flexible staffing: your floor shrinks when volume does, without you running a dozen off-cycle payrolls in January.

This article is general information, not legal or payroll advice. Confirm your specific obligations with your HR advisor or employment counsel.

The bottom line

In Arizona, a discharged worker's final pay is due within seven working days or by the next regular payday, whichever comes first. Plan the timing alongside your ramp-down schedule, handle sick time and rehires correctly and keep in touch with the people you want back.

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act on the Warehouse Floor: A Practical Guide

FLAT Staffing · November 25, 2026 · 4 min read

Physical jobs raise practical questions when an employee is pregnant. Can she keep picking orders that require lifting? What if she needs to sit more often, drink water on the line or take extra restroom breaks? What about a lot porter who spends the day walking hot pavement?

Since June 2023, a federal law has answered those questions more directly than before: the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). Many supervisors on warehouse floors and dealership lots still have not heard of it. Here is what it requires and how to handle requests well.

Who the law covers

According to the EEOC, the PWFA took effect on June 27, 2023. It applies to private and public employers with 15 or more employees, as well as employment agencies and labor organizations. The EEOC's implementing regulation took effect June 18, 2024.

The law requires covered employers to provide reasonable accommodations for a worker's known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, unless the accommodation would cause an undue hardship, meaning significant difficulty or expense.

What counts as a "known limitation"

The EEOC defines a limitation as a physical or mental condition related to pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions. It does not have to be severe. The EEOC gives examples like morning sickness and migraines, and notes that conditions can be minor or come and go. A limitation is "known" when the employee or their representative has communicated it to the employer.

No magic words are required. An employee saying "I'm pregnant and I can't lift those boxes right now" is enough to start the process.

Accommodations that fit physical jobs

The EEOC lists examples of reasonable accommodations. Several map directly onto warehouse, auction and dealership work:

  • Additional, longer or more flexible breaks to drink water, eat, rest or use the restroom
  • Allowing a water bottle or food in areas where policy normally prohibits it
  • A stool or chair, or the ability to alternate sitting and standing
  • Help with lifting or light duty
  • Modified uniforms, dress code or properly fitting safety equipment
  • Schedule changes, shorter hours, part-time work or a later start time
  • Temporary reassignment or temporary suspension of an essential job function
  • Leave for medical appointments or recovery from childbirth

The "temporarily unable" rule

One feature of the PWFA is different from the Americans with Disabilities Act. Under the PWFA, a worker can still be considered qualified even if she temporarily cannot perform an essential function of the job, as long as the inability is temporary, she could perform the function in the near future and the inability can be reasonably accommodated.

For a forklift operator or order picker, that may mean moving her to a less physical task for a period, such as scanning, labeling, cycle counts or returns processing, rather than taking her off the schedule.

What employers must not do

The EEOC highlights several prohibited actions. Employers may not:

  • Deny a reasonable accommodation that would not cause undue hardship
  • Force a worker to accept an accommodation that was not arrived at through discussion with her
  • Deny a job or opportunity because of the need for an accommodation
  • Require leave when another accommodation would let her keep working
  • Retaliate against someone for requesting an accommodation or reporting a violation

The leave point matters most in practice. Sending a pregnant employee home "for her own safety" when she could keep working with a modified task is the kind of decision the law was written to stop.

Keep the process simple

The EEOC expects the interactive process to be quick in many cases, often a short conversation or email. A few practical guidelines:

  • Respond promptly. Delays can themselves become a problem.
  • Limit documentation. The EEOC says employers generally should not require medical documentation when the need is obvious or already known, or for common requests like extra restroom breaks, water or a stool. When documentation is appropriate, it should be limited to confirming the condition and the change needed.
  • Keep medical information confidential.
  • Revisit as things change. Needs often change at different stages of pregnancy and after childbirth.

Related: lactation breaks

After the baby arrives, the federal PUMP Act separately requires reasonable break time and a private space other than a bathroom for nursing employees, for up to one year after birth. Plan the space in advance.

When the worker is a temp

The PWFA applies to employment agencies as well as employers, and in practice both the staffing agency and the host site usually have a role. The agency receives the request and manages the employment relationship. The host controls the tasks, schedule and floor.

We suggest agreeing in advance with your staffing partner on:

  • Who an assigned worker should tell when she needs an accommodation
  • How quickly the host will respond about task changes or seating
  • Which alternative tasks are available on site
  • How confidentiality will be maintained

This article is general information, not legal advice. The EEOC has signaled it may revisit parts of its PWFA regulation, though the law itself remains in effect. Confirm current obligations with employment counsel or the EEOC.

The bottom line

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act asks employers to do something most good supervisors already want to do: find a practical way for a pregnant worker to keep working safely. Train your leads to recognize a request, respond quickly, avoid forcing leave and coordinate with your staffing partner when the worker is a temp.

If you want help planning flexible task assignments on your floor, talk with our team or call 602-730-3312.

Marijuana and Drug Testing in Arizona: What Employers Can Still Do

FLAT Staffing · November 23, 2026 · 5 min read

Since Arizona voters approved recreational marijuana in 2020, we have heard a version of the same question from almost every client with forklifts, yard trucks or customer vehicles on site: can we still test, and what happens if someone tests positive?

The short answer is yes, employers in Arizona keep substantial rights. But the details depend on whether you have a written policy, whether the person is a medical marijuana cardholder and whether the job is safety-sensitive. Here is a practical overview for Phoenix-area operations.

What Prop 207 does and does not change

The Smart and Safe Arizona Act (Proposition 207) is codified in A.R.S. Title 36, Chapter 28.2. Its text includes several provisions that preserve employer rights. According to A.R.S. 36-2851, the law:

  • Does not restrict employers' rights to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace
  • Does not affect employers' ability to adopt policies restricting marijuana use by employees or prospective employees
  • Does not require employers to allow or accommodate marijuana use, possession or cultivation in the workplace
  • Allows property owners and businesses to prohibit or regulate otherwise legal conduct on their property

The same statute keeps it illegal to drive or operate a vehicle while impaired "to even the slightest degree" by marijuana. For dealership porters, auction drivers and anyone operating equipment, that matters.

In short, legal recreational use did not create a right to use marijuana at work or to show up impaired.

Medical marijuana cardholders are different

Arizona's older medical marijuana law adds protections that recreational users do not have. Under A.R.S. 36-2813, unless an exception applies, an employer may not:

  • Discriminate in hiring, termination or terms of employment based on someone's status as a registered cardholder
  • Penalize a registered qualifying patient for a positive test for marijuana components or metabolites, unless the patient used, possessed or was impaired by marijuana on the premises or during work hours

There is also an exception when following these rules would cause an employer to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations. Employers with federally regulated drivers or federal contracts should get advice on how that interacts with their programs.

The practical takeaway: a positive marijuana test alone is not always enough to act against a cardholder. You need to look at impairment and on-the-job use.

Arizona's drug testing law: the policy matters

Arizona has a drug testing statute, A.R.S. 23-493 and following, that gives employers legal protection when they test under a compliant written policy. Under A.R.S. 23-493.04, the policy must be in writing and distributed to employees (or made available the same way as other personnel policies), and applicants must be told they will be tested. The policy should cover:

  1. Your drug and alcohol policy statement
  2. Who is subject to testing
  3. When testing may happen
  4. Which substances are tested
  5. Testing methods and collection procedures
  6. Consequences of refusing a test
  7. Possible discipline based on results
  8. The employee's right to get written results on request
  9. The employee's right to confidentially explain a positive result
  10. Your confidentiality policy for results

The statute allows testing for job-related reasons, including possible impairment, workplace accidents (for employees reasonably believed to have contributed, as soon as practicable), safety, productivity and reasonable suspicion. Random testing is permitted. And if you adopt an impairment testing policy, all compensated employees, including supervisors and officers, must be uniformly covered.

Impairment and safety-sensitive roles

A.R.S. 23-493.06 protects employers who have a compliant policy when they act on a good-faith belief that an employee was impaired at work or used drugs on the premises or during work hours. It also allows employers to remove someone from a safety-sensitive position, by reassignment or leave, based on a good-faith belief of current drug use that could cause impairment, whether the drug is legal, prescribed or otherwise.

The statute lists what a good-faith belief can be based on, including test results, warning labels, the employee's own statements, a physician or pharmacist's advice and other reliable information.

For most of the roles we staff, from forklift operators to lot drivers, it is worth defining in your policy which positions you treat as safety-sensitive and why.

Post-accident testing and OSHA

OSHA's injury reporting rules prohibit retaliating against employees for reporting injuries. In a 2018 memo, OSHA clarified that most workplace drug testing is permissible, including random testing, testing unrelated to injury reporting, testing required by state workers' compensation law or federal rules, and post-incident testing to find the root cause of an incident. OSHA said the employer should test everyone whose conduct could have contributed, not only the person who reported an injury. A testing program violates the rule only if it is used to penalize someone for reporting.

Temps: who tests?

When you use a staffing agency, the agency is the employer of record and typically runs pre-assignment and post-incident testing under its own policy. Agree with your partner on:

  • Which assignments require pre-assignment testing and which panel is used
  • How reasonable-suspicion and post-incident tests are triggered on your site
  • How results are communicated and kept confidential
  • What happens when a worker is removed from an assignment

This article is general information, not legal advice. Drug testing law has many details, especially for medical cardholders and federally regulated roles. Consult employment counsel before adopting or changing a policy.

The bottom line

Legal marijuana did not take away an Arizona employer's right to a drug-free workplace. What protects you is a written policy that follows the state statute, uniform application, careful handling of medical cardholders and clear documentation of impairment.

Safety Training Workers Actually Understand: OSHA's Language and Comprehension Rule

FLAT Staffing · November 20, 2026 · 4 min read

Peak season fills a building with new faces fast. A lot of them are temporary, many are new to the site and some are more comfortable in Spanish or another language than in English. That puts pressure on one of the least glamorous parts of safety: training. A signed attendance sheet from a 20-minute English-only video does not mean anyone learned anything.

OSHA has a clear position on this, and it is worth revisiting before your next onboarding wave.

The rule: training has to be understood

OSHA's list of employer responsibilities includes a line that surprises some managers: provide employee safety training in a language and vocabulary employees can understand.

OSHA spelled this out in an April 2010 policy memo to its regional offices. The memo says that whenever an OSHA standard requires training or instruction, OSHA interprets that to mean the information must be presented in a manner employees are capable of understanding. Key points from the memo:

  • Language. If an employee does not speak or understand English, training must be provided in a language the employee understands. Employers may also offer English instruction, but it does not replace training the worker can actually follow.
  • Vocabulary. Training must account for an employee's limited vocabulary. Technical jargon can be as much of a barrier as a different language.
  • Literacy. Handing written material to someone who cannot read it does not satisfy the training requirement.
  • Consistency. If you routinely give work instructions in a particular language or at a particular vocabulary level, OSHA expects safety training to be delivered the same way.

What inspectors look for

The memo directs compliance officers to go beyond checking whether training records exist. They are told to verify that training was presented in a form employees could understand. If an officer finds that training was not conveyed in an understandable way, the memo says the violation may be cited as serious.

The memo also notes that an employer may not rely on a work rule it never communicated in a language the employee could understand. In other words, "we told them" only counts if they could understand what you said.

Arizona runs its own state OSHA plan through ADOSH, part of the Industrial Commission of Arizona. State plans are required to be at least as effective as federal OSHA, so plan on the same expectation here.

Temp workers: whose job is it?

Training is one of the areas where staffing agencies and host employers share responsibility. OSHA's guidance on temporary workers says, in general:

  • The staffing agency is responsible for making sure its workers are properly trained, and needs a reasonable basis to believe the host's site-specific training covers the hazards workers will face.
  • The host employer usually provides workplace-specific training, because it knows and controls the hazards on its floor.
  • On hazard communication, the host has the primary role, since it controls the chemicals and hazards; the agency must at least inform its workers about the standard's requirements.

OSHA recommends that both parties put these duties in writing. The language question belongs in that conversation. If your site training is English-only and the crew coming in is mostly Spanish-speaking, both companies have a problem.

Practical ways to get it right

You do not need a professional translation department. You need a process that confirms people understood.

  1. Know your crew. Ask at onboarding which language each person is most comfortable with. Your staffing partner should already know this for the workers it sends.
  2. Train in that language. Use bilingual trainers or leads for live instruction. OSHA publishes many resources in Spanish that can supplement your site material.
  3. Keep the vocabulary plain. "Stay out of the forklift lane" beats "maintain separation from powered industrial truck travel paths."
  4. Show, don't just tell. Walk the floor. Point out the emergency exits, eyewash stations, pedestrian lanes and lockout points. Demonstrate the safe way to lift, cut stretch wrap or work a dock plate.
  5. Check understanding. Ask people to explain or demonstrate back. Some OSHA standards already require employers to verify that employees learned the material.
  6. Match signage. If training is bilingual, make key signs and labels bilingual too.
  7. Document it. Record the language used, who trained, what was covered and how understanding was checked. That record is far more useful than a signature alone.
  8. Repeat it. Peak brings new people every week. Build short refreshers into shift starts instead of front-loading everything on day one.

Why this pays off

Clear training is not only about avoiding citations. New workers have the least experience with your hazards, and peak volume leaves little room for error. When people understand the rules, they follow them more consistently, they ask questions sooner and supervisors spend less time correcting the same mistakes.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Consult your safety professional or counsel about your specific obligations.

The bottom line

OSHA expects safety training to be understood, not just delivered. Train in a language and vocabulary your crew can follow, check that it landed, document how you did it and agree in writing with your staffing partner on who covers what.

Breaks and Meal Periods in Arizona: What's Required and What Must Be Paid

FLAT Staffing · November 18, 2026 · 5 min read

Ask ten supervisors whether Arizona requires a lunch break and you will get several different answers. Many people assume the rules are like California's. They are not. But "not required" does not mean "anything goes." Federal law decides which breaks count as paid time, and a separate federal law protects break time for nursing employees.

During peak, when shifts run long and supervisors are juggling coverage, these details are easy to get wrong. Here is a clear rundown for Phoenix-area operations.

Arizona does not require meal or rest breaks for adults

The U.S. Department of Labor maintains tables of state meal period and rest period laws for private-sector employers. Arizona does not appear in either table for adult workers. DOL's rest period table notes that states not listed do not require paid rest periods.

The federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) does not require lunch or coffee breaks either. So for adult employees in Arizona, whether to offer breaks, and how many, is generally up to the employer.

Most employers offer them anyway, for good reason. People working a 10-hour shift on a pick line or a hot auction lot need rest to stay safe and productive. And once you offer breaks, the federal rules below apply.

Short breaks must be paid

DOL guidance is clear: rest periods of short duration, usually 20 minutes or less, must be counted as hours worked. That means:

  • They must be paid.
  • They count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold.
  • You cannot clock people out for a 10- or 15-minute break and treat it as unpaid.

This catches employers who use automated timekeeping that deducts every punch-out. If someone punches out for a 12-minute break, that time still has to be paid.

Meal periods can be unpaid, if they are real

A bona fide meal period, typically 30 minutes or more, generally does not need to be paid. The key condition, per DOL, is that the employee must be completely relieved from duty for the purpose of eating a regular meal.

That condition is where problems start. A meal period is not truly off duty if the employee is:

  • Expected to watch the dock door or answer the radio
  • Required to stay at a workstation
  • Interrupted to help with a rush and then sent back to finish eating

If any of that is routine, the time may be compensable. Train supervisors to leave people alone during unpaid meals, or to pay the time when they cannot.

Other time that often gets missed

DOL's hours-worked guidance also covers situations common in warehouses and lots:

  • Waiting time. If an employee is "engaged to wait," such as being told to stand by until a trailer arrives, that is work time.
  • On-call time on premises. If you require someone to stay on site on call, that time counts.
  • Required training. Training generally counts as work time unless it is outside normal hours, voluntary, not job-related and no other work is done during it.
  • The workday. The workday runs from the first principal activity to the last, which may be longer than the scheduled shift.

Lactation breaks are required

The PUMP for Nursing Mothers Act expanded federal break time protections in December 2022. According to DOL, nearly all FLSA-covered employees who need to express breast milk are entitled to:

  • Reasonable break time each time they need to pump, for up to one year after the child's birth
  • A private space that is not a bathroom, shielded from view and free from intrusion by coworkers and the public

On pay: pump breaks can be unpaid only if the employee is completely relieved from duty. If you pay other breaks, pump breaks taken during those breaks must be paid the same way, and any work done while pumping must be paid.

Employers with fewer than 50 employees can claim an exemption only if compliance would cause undue hardship, which is judged by significant difficulty or expense relative to the employer's size and resources. It is not an automatic small-business exemption.

For warehouses and dealerships, the space requirement takes some planning. A locking office, a converted storage room or a dedicated room near the floor can work. A restroom stall cannot.

Minors are different

Some states set break rules for workers under 18, and federal law sets hours limits for younger teens. If you are bringing on 16- or 17-year-olds for winter break, check the youth rules separately. We cover those in a separate post.

What we recommend

  1. Write a break policy that says how many breaks, how long, and which are paid. Apply it to everyone on site, including temps.
  2. Pay all breaks of 20 minutes or less. Check that your timekeeping system does not deduct them.
  3. Protect unpaid meals. If supervisors regularly interrupt meals, either stop the interruptions or pay the time.
  4. Set up a lactation space before anyone asks for it, and tell supervisors how to handle requests.
  5. Align with your staffing partner. The agency pays temps, so it needs accurate punches and should know your break schedule. Make sure everyone's records match.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Confirm your specific obligations with your HR advisor or employment counsel.

The bottom line

Arizona leaves break schedules to employers, but federal law still decides what counts as paid time. Pay short breaks, keep meal periods truly off duty, provide lactation breaks and space, and make sure your timekeeping matches your policy.

Peak-Season Attendance Bonuses and Overtime: Getting the Regular Rate Right

FLAT Staffing · November 16, 2026 · 5 min read

Peak season brings out the incentives. Perfect-attendance bonuses for the week of Black Friday. A dollar more an hour for anyone who works every scheduled shift through December. A safety bonus for a crew that goes the month without an incident. These programs work. They also change how much overtime you owe, and that part is easy to miss.

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), overtime is not simply one and a half times the base hourly wage. It is one and a half times the regular rate, and most bonuses get folded into that number. Here is how it works and how to keep your peak incentives from turning into back-pay claims.

What the regular rate includes

The Department of Labor's guidance starts with a simple rule: bonuses are part of the regular rate unless a specific exclusion applies. DOL Fact Sheet #56C lists common bonuses that must be included, because they are promised in advance and employees expect them:

  • Attendance bonuses
  • Production bonuses based on a formula, individual or group
  • Quality and accuracy bonuses
  • Bonuses announced to encourage faster or more efficient work
  • Safety bonuses, such as for a number of days without an incident

The fact sheet adds a point employers sometimes argue with: the fact that you could decide not to pay a promised bonus does not make it discretionary.

DOL confirmed this again in 2026

In January 2026, DOL's Wage and Hour Division issued Opinion Letter FLSA2026-2 on an incentive program that paid drivers extra per hour based on punctuality, attendance, safety tasks and efficiency. The employer had been calculating overtime on the base wage alone. DOL concluded the bonuses were nondiscretionary, because the terms were set in advance, and had to be included in the regular rate for each week they were earned.

How the math works

Here is the example from DOL Fact Sheet #56C. An employee earns $10 an hour, works 43 hours and earns a $50 nondiscretionary bonus that week.

  • Straight-time pay: $10 x 43 = $430
  • Add the bonus: $430 + $50 = $480
  • Regular rate: $480 / 43 = $11.16
  • Half-time premium: $11.16 x 0.5 = $5.58
  • Overtime premium for 3 hours: $16.74
  • Total due: $496.74

If the employer had ignored the bonus and paid overtime on $10 alone, it would have paid $15 in overtime premium instead of $16.74. A small gap on one paycheck. Across a few hundred workers and six weeks of peak, it adds up, and back wages under the FLSA can come with liquidated damages.

The opinion letter shows the same effect at a larger scale. A worker earning $12 an hour plus $5.60 an hour in bonuses for a 50-hour week has a regular rate of $17.60, which means an $8.80 half-time premium on each of the 10 overtime hours, or $968 in total wages for the week.

Bonuses that cover more than one week

Some incentives are paid at the end of a period, such as "work every scheduled shift from Thanksgiving through New Year's and receive $300." Federal regulations allow you to pay overtime on the base rate during the period and then, once the bonus is earned, apportion it back over the weeks it covers and pay extra overtime for the weeks that had overtime hours. If you can't tell how much of the bonus was earned in each week, the regulation allows a reasonable method, such as assuming it was earned evenly across the weeks or hours.

In practice, that means a true-up payment after the bonus period ends. Build it into your payroll calendar so it doesn't get forgotten in January.

What can be excluded

Not every payment raises the regular rate. Under DOL guidance, these can generally be left out:

  • Discretionary bonuses, but only if you keep sole discretion over whether to pay and how much until at or near the end of the period, and the bonus is not paid under a prior promise. A thank-you bonus decided after peak, with no advance announcement, can fit. A bonus you advertised in October does not.
  • Holiday gifts that are not tied to hours worked, production or efficiency, such as the same gift card for everyone.
  • Holiday and weekend premiums paid at one and a half times the normal rate or more, which can also be credited toward overtime owed.

The label you put on a payment does not decide the question. DOL looks at the facts.

A connection to the new overtime deduction

There is one more reason to get the regular rate right this year. Starting with 2026 wages, employers must report "qualified overtime compensation" on Form W-2 for the federal no-tax-on-overtime deduction. That amount is the FLSA-required premium, calculated from the regular rate. If your regular rate is understated, the figure you report will be too. We cover the W-2 side in a separate post next month.

How to run peak incentives cleanly

  1. Write the rules down. Spell out eligibility, the amount and the period. Clarity helps attendance and makes payroll easier.
  2. Tell payroll before the program starts, so bonuses are coded as nondiscretionary and included in overtime calculations automatically.
  3. Plan the true-up for any multi-week bonus.
  4. Use a premium of at least time and a half if you want to pay extra for holiday shifts and credit it toward overtime.
  5. Coordinate with your staffing partner. If you want temps included in an incentive, the agency pays it as employer of record and must include it in their regular rate. Agree in writing on the terms and how it will be billed, including the overtime effect.

This article is general information, not legal or payroll advice. Confirm your specific situation with your payroll provider or employment counsel.

The bottom line

Peak incentives are a good tool for keeping shifts covered. Just remember that a promised bonus is part of pay, and pay above 40 hours carries a premium. Include nondiscretionary bonuses in the regular rate, true up multi-week bonuses and make sure your staffing partner does the same.

Holiday Pay in Arizona: What the Law Requires for Thanksgiving and Christmas Shifts

FLAT Staffing · November 13, 2026 · 5 min read

Every November we get the same set of questions from operations managers: Do we have to pay time and a half on Thanksgiving? If we close for Christmas, do hourly people get paid? Does holiday pay count toward overtime? With distribution centers running hard through the holidays and dealerships pushing year-end sales, the answers matter for both budgets and morale.

Here is what federal and Arizona law actually require, and where the overtime math gets tricky.

The short answer: holiday pay is not required

The U.S. Department of Labor is direct about it: the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) does not require payment for time not worked, such as vacations or holidays. Those benefits are a matter of agreement between the employer and the employee.

The FLSA also does not require a premium rate for working on a holiday. Thanksgiving is treated like any other day for federal wage purposes. If a non-exempt employee works on Thanksgiving, you owe at least their regular rate, and overtime applies only if they go over 40 hours in the workweek.

Arizona does not add a private-sector holiday pay requirement. The state's wage laws focus on minimum wage, earned paid sick time and timely payment of wages. So for most Phoenix-area employers, holiday pay is a policy choice, not a legal mandate.

The exception is federal contract work. DOL notes that contracts covered by the Service Contract Act can carry holiday fringe benefit requirements in their wage determinations. If you hold federal contracts, check yours.

Where holiday pay meets overtime

Even though holiday pay is optional, once you offer it, federal overtime rules shape how it works.

Paid holidays you don't work do not count as hours worked

If you give hourly employees eight hours of paid holiday on Christmas Day while the building is closed, that pay is excluded from the regular rate and those hours do not count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold. Federal regulations treat pay for holidays not worked as not compensation for working, so it also cannot be credited toward overtime you owe.

Example: an employee gets 8 hours of holiday pay and works 36 hours the rest of the week. Total paid hours are 44, but hours worked are 36, so no overtime is owed under the FLSA. (Your own policy may be more generous.)

Holiday premium pay can be credited toward overtime

Many employers pay time and a half or double time for working a holiday. DOL's overtime guidance says extra pay for work on holidays, weekends or rest days, at a rate of at least one and a half times the normal rate, can be excluded from the regular rate and credited toward overtime owed that week.

Premiums below time and a half work differently, so if you pay something like a flat extra dollar an hour for holiday shifts, have payroll review how it is treated.

Holiday gifts vs. bonuses

DOL allows employers to exclude genuine gifts from the regular rate. A holiday gift qualifies when it is a reward for service and is not measured by or dependent on hours worked, production or efficiency. A same-amount gift card for everyone at the holiday party fits. A "work every shift through December 31 and get $200" payment does not; that is an attendance bonus, which must be included in the regular rate for overtime.

Earned paid sick time around the holidays

Arizona's earned paid sick time law still applies during the holidays. Employees can use accrued time for qualifying reasons, including their own illness or caring for a family member. Be careful with blanket rules like "no sick time the day before or after a holiday." Policies that discourage legitimate use of protected sick time can create problems. If you see attendance patterns that concern you, talk with your HR advisor about what documentation rules allow.

Policy decisions to make now

If you have not settled your holiday policy for this season, here is what we suggest deciding and communicating before Thanksgiving week:

  1. Which days are paid holidays, if any, and who is eligible (full-time only, after a waiting period, and so on).
  2. What rate applies to holiday shifts. If you pay a premium, consider making it at least time and a half so it can be credited toward overtime.
  3. How holiday pay affects overtime. Put the rule in writing: paid holiday hours not worked do not count toward 40, unless you choose to be more generous.
  4. Scheduling and volunteers. Decide how you will staff Thanksgiving, Black Friday, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve, and whether you will ask for volunteers first.
  5. Temp workers. Holiday pay for agency workers follows the staffing agency's policy and your bill rate agreement. If you want temps to receive a holiday premium, agree on it with your agency in advance so it shows up correctly on both the paycheck and the invoice.

Why it matters on the floor

Holiday policy is a retention tool as much as a payroll rule. In a tight market, the warehouse down the road offering a holiday premium can pull people off your schedule for the busiest week of the year. Clear, consistent holiday rules, announced early, help people plan and help you staff.

This article is general information, not legal or payroll advice. Confirm your specific obligations with your HR advisor or employment counsel.

The bottom line

Neither federal nor Arizona law requires holiday pay or a holiday premium for private employers. But once you offer either, the FLSA's overtime rules decide how it is counted. Decide your policy, put it in writing and make sure your staffing partner bills and pays it the same way.

Background Checks for Warehouse and Dealership Hires: FCRA Basics for Employers

FLAT Staffing · November 11, 2026 · 5 min read

Background checks are routine for a lot of the roles we fill. Dealerships want them for lot drivers and porters who handle keys and vehicles. Distribution centers want them for people who work around high-value inventory. Auction clients want them for anyone moving customer cars. The check itself is usually quick. The paperwork around it is where employers get into trouble.

When you use an outside company to run a background check, a federal law called the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) applies, and the Federal Trade Commission has published clear guidance on what employers have to do. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) adds a second layer: how you use the results. Here is a practical overview.

When the FCRA applies

The FCRA covers "consumer reports" prepared by a consumer reporting agency, which includes most third-party background screening companies. If you pay a screening vendor to pull criminal records, verify employment or compile other background information for a hiring decision, assume the FCRA applies and follow its steps.

Before you run the check

According to the FTC, an employer must do three things before getting a consumer report on an applicant or employee:

  1. Give a written disclosure in a stand-alone document. The notice that you may use a report for employment decisions cannot be buried inside the job application. It has to stand on its own.
  2. Get written authorization. The person must give permission in writing. The authorization can be on the same document as the disclosure. If you want the permission to cover checks throughout employment, the FTC says that should be stated clearly and conspicuously.
  3. Certify to the screening company. You confirm to the vendor that you gave notice, got permission, will follow the FCRA and will not misuse the information in violation of equal opportunity laws.

There are extra notice requirements for "investigative" reports, which are based on personal interviews about someone's character or reputation. Most standard criminal and employment checks are not investigative reports, but confirm with your vendor which type you are ordering.

Before you say no: the pre-adverse action notice

This is the step that gets skipped most often. If something in the report might lead you to not hire someone, withdraw an offer or take other adverse action, the FTC says you must first give the person:

  • A notice that includes a copy of the report you relied on
  • A copy of "A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act"

The point is to give the person a chance to review the report and dispute anything inaccurate before the decision is final. Records do get mixed up, especially with common names. A short pause here protects both of you.

After the decision: the adverse action notice

Once you make a final decision, you must notify the person orally, in writing or electronically. Per the FTC, that notice must include:

  • The name, address and phone number of the screening company that supplied the report
  • A statement that the screening company did not make the decision and cannot explain why it was made
  • Notice of the person's right to dispute the accuracy or completeness of the information, and to get a free additional report from the company if they ask within 60 days

How you use the results: EEOC guidance

The FCRA governs the process. Federal anti-discrimination law governs how you use what you learn. The EEOC's guidance for employers makes a few points that matter for high-volume hourly hiring:

  • Apply the same standards to everyone. Rejecting one applicant for a record while hiring another with a similar record is evidence of discrimination.
  • Watch for disparate impact. A policy that screens out people with certain records can be unlawful if it disproportionately excludes a protected group and is not job related and consistent with business necessity.
  • Tie the standard to the job. A recent theft conviction may be relevant for someone handling inventory or vehicle keys. The same record may say much less about someone sorting returns. Think about what the role actually involves.
  • Consider disability-related explanations. If a background problem was caused by a disability, the EEOC says to give the person a chance to show they can still do the job, unless that would cause significant difficulty or expense.

Keep and dispose of records properly

The EEOC says employers generally must keep application and hiring records, including those for people not hired, for one year from when they were made or the personnel action was taken, whichever is later. If a discrimination charge is filed, keep records until the matter is resolved.

When the retention period ends, the FTC's disposal rule requires secure destruction: shredding, burning or pulverizing paper, and destroying electronic files so they cannot be read or reconstructed.

A note on driving roles

For lot drivers, porters and auction drivers, many employers also review driving history. If a screening company supplies that driving record, treat it like any other report from that vendor and follow the same notice and authorization steps. Set your driving standards in writing before you start reviewing records, and apply them consistently.

How this works when you use a staffing agency

When temporary workers come through an agency, the agency is the employer of record and typically orders the checks, collects the authorizations and handles the notices. As the client, you usually define the screening standard for your site.

A few questions worth asking any staffing partner, including us:

  1. Who orders the check, and which screening company is used?
  2. What exactly is included (counties, years of history, driving record, employment verification)?
  3. Do you send pre-adverse and adverse action notices every time, with the required documents?
  4. Is our screening standard written down, and is it applied the same way to every candidate?
  5. What happens when we convert a temp to direct hire? If you want your own check at conversion, you will need your own disclosure and authorization.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Background check rules can also vary by state and city, so confirm your obligations with employment counsel.

The bottom line

A background check takes a few days. A sloppy process can create exposure that lasts years. Use a stand-alone disclosure, get written authorization, send both notices before and after any adverse decision, and apply a written, job-related standard to every candidate.

Q1 2027 Staffing Readiness Checklist for Phoenix Employers

FLAT Staffing · November 9, 2026 · 4 min read

January has a way of arriving all at once. Peak wraps up, returns pile in, a new minimum wage takes effect, budgets reset and the first planning meetings for summer start before anyone has caught their breath. A little preparation in November and December makes the first quarter much smoother.

Here is the checklist we suggest Phoenix-area operations, HR and site leaders work through before January 1, 2027. Print it, share it with your team and check items off as you go.

1. Pay and budget

  • Apply the 2027 minimum wage. Arizona's minimum wage is set to rise to $15.65 per hour on January 1, 2027, based on the CPI formula in A.R.S. 23-363. Confirm the official notice from the Industrial Commission of Arizona and update payroll systems before the first pay period.
  • Address wage compression. Decide whether pay bands above the floor will move, and communicate changes before they take effect.
  • Update loaded labor costs. Include payroll taxes and workers' comp in your cost per hour.
  • Confirm 2027 bill rates. If you use a staffing partner, get updated rates in writing for any roles affected by the new minimum.
  • Check local rules. If you operate in Flagstaff or Tucson, confirm their separate local minimums.

2. Posters, documents and policies

  • Replace required workplace posters with current versions, including the Arizona minimum wage and earned paid sick time notice.
  • Review offer letters and job postings for outdated pay rates.
  • Review your earned paid sick time policy. Confirm accrual, caps, carryover and your benefit year align with A.R.S. 23-372 and that pay stubs show the required information.
  • Refresh your handbook. Make sure anti-harassment, safety and reporting procedures are current and apply to everyone on site, including temps.

3. Hiring and verification

  • Confirm your Form I-9 edition. Use the current version from USCIS and watch posted expiration dates.
  • Audit your E-Verify process. Arizona requires E-Verify for all new hires. Confirm cases are created consistently and on time.
  • Plan for temp-to-hire conversions. If you plan to convert seasonal temps in January, remember you will need to complete your own I-9 and E-Verify case for each conversion.
  • Ask your staffing partner for proof of E-Verify enrollment if you have not done so recently.

4. Safety and heat planning

  • Review your 2026 incident data. Look for patterns in injuries and near misses during peak.
  • Write or update your Heat Illness Prevention Plan. Arizona's Workplace Heat Safety Task Force recommendations were approved by the Industrial Commission in April 2026, and ADOSH continues its Heat Stress State Emphasis Program. Use the cooler months to update your plan, using the ADOSH template if helpful.
  • Schedule heat training before May. Include supervisors, new hires and temporary workers.
  • Plan acclimatization. Map out how new and returning workers will be phased into hot conditions.
  • Clarify temp safety responsibilities. Confirm in writing who provides site-specific training, PPE and injury reporting with your staffing partner.

5. Workforce planning

  • Run a peak post-mortem. What went well, where were you short, which shifts had the most no-shows and how long did it take to fill gaps?
  • Forecast Q1 volume by week. Include returns season in distribution, and auction and dealership volume patterns for automotive operations.
  • Set baseline and flex headcount. Staff your core for steady volume and plan flexible labor for spikes.
  • Identify your keepers. Flag top seasonal performers you want to retain, convert or bring back next peak.
  • Map automation changes. If new equipment or systems go live in 2027, plan training and transition labor now.

6. Market awareness

  • Benchmark pay. Check current BLS occupational wage data and local job postings for the roles you hire most.
  • Track the local market. Note the Phoenix metro unemployment rate and employment trends in your industry through BLS and the Arizona Office of Economic Opportunity.
  • Watch major employers nearby. New distribution centers, manufacturing ramp-ups and construction projects in your corridor can affect your applicant flow.

7. Staffing partner review

  • Review performance. Fill rate, time to fill, attendance and early turnover for the past year.
  • Confirm insurance. Request current certificates of insurance for workers' comp and general liability.
  • Revisit the agreement. Check scope of work, training responsibilities, injury reporting, conversion terms and how hiring and discipline decisions are handled.
  • Share your 2027 plan. Give your partner your volume forecast, upcoming projects and roles you expect to need, so they can build a bench ahead of time.

8. Legal and regulatory watch list

Keep an eye on these items in 2027:

  • Federal joint employer rule. The Department of Labor proposed a new joint employer rule in April 2026. Watch for whether it is finalized.
  • Federal heat standard. OSHA's proposed heat rule has not been finalized. OSHA's updated heat emphasis program remains in effect.
  • Arizona heat guidance. ADOSH is updating its emphasis program based on the 2026 guidelines.

This checklist is general information, not legal advice. Consult your HR advisor or employment counsel about your specific obligations.

The bottom line

The first quarter sets the tone for the year. Pay changes, compliance updates, heat planning and a clear workforce plan are much easier to handle in November than in mid-January.
