Reading the Phoenix Labor Market: Where to Find Reliable Data and How to Use It

FLAT Staffing · November 6, 2026 · 4 min read

Every operations manager has heard a version of "the labor market is tight" or "the labor market is loosening." Those statements are only useful if you know what is behind them and how they apply to your building, your roles and your part of the Valley.

The good news is that some of the best labor market data available is free, public and updated regularly. Here is where to find it and how we suggest using it.

The two main sources

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)

The BLS produces the core federal labor statistics, many of them in partnership with state agencies. For Phoenix, the easiest starting point is the Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler Economy at a Glance page, which pulls together the main metro-level series in one place.

Arizona Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO)

The OEO is Arizona's state labor market information office. Its labor market section publishes industry employment and wages, occupational wages by county, unemployment and labor force trends for counties, cities and towns, and two-year and ten-year employment projections. The OEO also publishes a release schedule so you know when new numbers are coming.

The data series worth knowing

You do not need to become an economist. A handful of series will cover most planning needs.

Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)

LAUS provides labor force, employment and unemployment rates for states, metro areas, counties and many cities. It is the source of the metro unemployment rate you see in the news. For example, the BLS reported Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler unemployment at 4.9 percent for August 2026 (preliminary, not seasonally adjusted).

How to use it: Unemployment trends give a broad sense of how many people are looking for work. A rising rate may make hiring easier; a falling one usually means more competition for workers.

Current Employment Statistics (CES)

CES measures payroll jobs by industry, including Trade, Transportation and Utilities, Manufacturing and Construction, at the metro level, every month.

How to use it: Watch the industries that compete with you for workers. If transportation and warehousing employment is growing fast, expect more competition for warehouse labor. If construction is booming, outdoor and general labor roles may get harder to fill.

Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS)

OEWS reports employment and wages for hundreds of specific occupations, such as laborers and freight movers, industrial truck operators and packers, at the state and metro level. It is published annually.

How to use it: OEWS is a solid benchmark for setting pay ranges. Compare your rates to the metro median and percentiles for the roles you hire. Remember it lags; the data reflects a reference period before publication, so adjust for wage growth since then.

Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)

QCEW counts employment and wages from unemployment insurance records, covering nearly all employers. It is very detailed by industry and county, but it is published with a lag of several months.

How to use it: Use QCEW to see longer-term industry trends in Maricopa County and to check average wages in your specific industry.

Consumer Price Index (CPI)

The BLS publishes CPI nationally and for the Phoenix area. The national CPI-U also drives Arizona's annual minimum wage adjustment under state law.

How to use it: Inflation affects what workers need to earn and how they view your pay. It also tells you in September what the next January minimum wage will be.

Turning data into decisions

Numbers are only useful if they change what you do. Here is how we suggest folding them into planning:

  1. Set a calendar. Check LAUS and CES monthly, OEWS when the annual release comes out and CPI each September for the minimum wage.
  2. Pick your comparison set. Track the two or three industries and five or so occupations that matter most to you. Ignore the rest.
  3. Benchmark pay once a year, at minimum. Use OEWS as a baseline and supplement it with what competitors are advertising locally.
  4. Compare with your own metrics. Applicant flow, time to fill, show rates and early turnover are your real-time labor market data. Public data explains the trend; your data tells you how it hits your operation.
  5. Plan scenarios. If unemployment rises a point, what happens to your applicant pool? If a major employer opens nearby, what does that do to your pay rate? Rough scenarios beat no plan.
  6. Share it with your staffing partner. A good agency sees applicant behavior across many clients and can add context to what the public data shows.

Common pitfalls

  • Comparing seasonally adjusted and unadjusted numbers. Metro data is often not seasonally adjusted, so compare the same month year over year.
  • Overreacting to one month. Monthly estimates are revised. Look at the trend over several months.
  • Treating the metro as one market. Labor conditions in the West Valley, East Valley and north Phoenix can differ. Commute patterns matter.
  • Using stale pay benchmarks. A wage survey from two years ago may be well below today's market.

The bottom line

Reliable labor market data for Phoenix is free and easy to access once you know where to look. Combine BLS and OEO data with your own hiring metrics, and you will make better decisions on pay, timing and headcount.

TSMC Arizona and the Phoenix Chip Build-Out: What It Means for the Local Labor Market

FLAT Staffing · November 4, 2026 · 4 min read

The semiconductor build-out in north Phoenix is the largest industrial project most of us will see in our careers. Even if your business has nothing to do with chips, it is changing the labor market you hire from. Construction crews, suppliers, logistics providers and service companies are all growing around it, and they are recruiting from the same Valley workforce you are.

Here is what is confirmed about the project and how we think about its effect on Phoenix-area employers.

The scale of TSMC Arizona

According to TSMC's official Arizona site:

  • TSMC's planned investment in Arizona has grown from an initial $12 billion to $265 billion, which the company describes as the largest foreign direct investment in a greenfield project in U.S. history.
  • The full plan includes six wafer fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and an R&D center.
  • Fab 1 began high-volume production on its N4 process in the fourth quarter of 2024.
  • Fab 2 completed structural construction in 2025, with volume production targeted for the second half of 2027.
  • Fab 3 broke ground in April 2025.
  • Construction on Fab 4 and the first advanced packaging facility began in early 2026.
  • TSMC Arizona reports more than 3,500 employees, and the company expects the first three fabs to create about 6,000 direct high-tech jobs, plus construction and supplier jobs.

In March 2025, when TSMC announced a $100 billion expansion of its U.S. plans, the company said that expansion was expected to support roughly 40,000 construction jobs over four years.

How a project this size affects the labor market

The direct fab jobs are mostly specialized: engineers, technicians and equipment specialists. The wider ripple effect is what matters for most Valley employers.

Construction pulls from general labor

Multi-year construction of fabs and support facilities requires large crews: laborers, equipment operators, electricians, pipefitters and support staff. Construction support work can compete for the same people who might otherwise work in warehouses or on auction lots, particularly those who are comfortable with outdoor, physical work.

Suppliers and logistics follow

Chip manufacturing relies on a network of chemical, gas, equipment and materials suppliers, plus the logistics companies that move those goods. As that network grows, it adds warehousing, distribution and transportation jobs in the region.

Technicians are in demand everywhere

Fabs need maintenance and facilities technicians, and so do automated warehouses, manufacturers and data centers. Employers across industries are recruiting from a similar pool of mechanically skilled workers.

Wage pressure spreads

When large employers raise pay for certain roles, nearby employers often feel it, especially those hiring for physically demanding or skilled hourly jobs. Even without precise data on the size of the effect, it is reasonable to expect continued competition for reliable hourly workers in the north and northwest Valley.

Housing and commute patterns shift

New jobs bring new residents, new housing and more traffic on key corridors. Commute time is one of the biggest factors in whether hourly workers stay, so changes in where people live and how they travel can affect attendance and retention.

What this means for warehouse, auction and service employers

You do not have to be in the chip business to plan around it. A few practical moves:

  1. Watch the north and northwest Valley closely. If your operation sits along the I-17, Loop 303 or Deer Valley corridors, competition for hourly workers may be more intense than in other parts of the metro.
  2. Benchmark pay more often. Annual pay reviews may not be enough when a major employer nearby is ramping up. Check competitive rates quarterly.
  3. Make your jobs easy to start and easy to stay in. Clear schedules, predictable hours and good supervision help you compete without matching every dollar.
  4. Build a technician pipeline. Upskilling promising associates into maintenance roles is often more reliable than hiring experienced technicians on the open market.
  5. Use flexible labor for surges. A staffing partner with a broad pool can help cover peaks without overcommitting to permanent headcount in a tight market.
  6. Watch the data. Track Phoenix employment and wage trends through BLS and the Arizona Office of Economic Opportunity to see how the market is moving.

A longer-term opportunity

A major manufacturing anchor can also strengthen the regional economy over time: more training programs, more suppliers and more people moving to the Valley for work. Employers who invest in their own workforce now are better positioned to benefit from that growth rather than just compete with it.

The bottom line

TSMC Arizona's build-out is reshaping the Phoenix labor market well beyond the fab gates. Expect steady competition for hourly and technical workers, especially in the north Valley, and plan pay, retention and flexible staffing accordingly.

Warehouse Automation and What It Means for Labor Needs in Phoenix

FLAT Staffing · November 2, 2026 · 4 min read

Walk through a new distribution center in the West Valley today and you are likely to see some mix of conveyors, sortation, goods-to-person systems, autonomous mobile robots or automated storage. Ask the general manager whether that means fewer people, and the answer is usually more complicated than yes or no.

Here is our practical view of how automation is changing labor needs in Phoenix-area warehouses and how to plan around it.

Automation changes the work more than it removes it

In most facilities, automation targets specific bottlenecks: walking time in picking, manual sorting, repetitive lifting or inventory counts. When those tasks are automated, the jobs around them change.

Typical shifts we see:

  • Less walking, more station work. Goods-to-person systems bring product to a picker, so the job becomes faster-paced and more repetitive at a fixed station.
  • New exception handling. When a robot or sorter cannot process an item, a person has to resolve it. Exception handling takes judgment and system knowledge.
  • More technical roles. Maintenance technicians, controls specialists and system operators become critical, and they are harder to hire.
  • Different physical demands. Some heavy-lift tasks go away, while others, like induction onto conveyors, stay manual and can be fast and repetitive.

What usually stays manual

Even in highly automated buildings, several kinds of work remain people-driven:

  • Unloading floor-loaded trailers, especially with mixed or irregular freight
  • Handling odd-sized, fragile or high-value items
  • Returns processing, where every item needs inspection and a decision
  • Kitting, value-added services and custom packing
  • Quality checks and problem solving
  • Cleaning, replenishment and general facility support

Automation also tends to handle the steady baseline well but has fixed capacity. When volume spikes beyond what the system can process, operations often fall back on manual processes and additional labor to keep up.

Peaks still need people

This is one of the most important planning points. A sortation system rated for a certain throughput does not stretch on Cyber Monday. Many automated sites still bring on seasonal workers for peak, but they may need them in different roles: induction, exception handling, manual overflow lines and trailer unloading, rather than traditional walking pick paths.

The skills gap is real

Automation raises the bar for certain roles. Workers who interact with automated systems need to:

  • Follow on-screen instructions and scan-based workflows accurately
  • Recognize and report system faults
  • Work safely around moving equipment and robots
  • Adapt when processes change after a software update or system adjustment

Meanwhile, maintenance and controls technicians can be hard to find. In Phoenix, distribution centers often compete for those skill sets with the region's growing manufacturing and semiconductor employers.

How to plan your workforce around automation

If your facility is adding automation, or you are evaluating it, here is how we would approach workforce planning:

  1. Map tasks, not headcount. List every task in your process and mark which will be automated, which will change and which will stay manual. Headcount follows from that.
  2. Plan for the transition period. Go-lives rarely hit full throughput on day one. Budget for extra labor while systems ramp up and teams learn new processes.
  3. Identify your exception handlers. Pick people with good judgment and system aptitude and train them early.
  4. Invest in technician pipelines. Consider apprenticeships, partnerships with local community colleges or upskilling promising associates into maintenance roles.
  5. Rethink your flex labor profile. Tell your staffing partner which roles will need flexible labor after automation. The profile may shift from general pickers toward induction, unloading and returns.
  6. Update safety training. Robots and conveyors introduce new hazards: pinch points, traffic interaction and lockout/tagout. Everyone on site, including temps, needs that training.
  7. Measure the right things. Automated sites often track system uptime, exceptions per hour and throughput per labor hour rather than traditional pick rates.

What this means for temporary labor

Automation does not eliminate the need for flexible labor; it reshapes it. Automated sites tend to want temps who are:

  • Comfortable with scanners and screen-based instructions
  • Able to maintain pace at a fixed station
  • Safety conscious around equipment
  • Reliable enough to train once and bring back for each peak

That last point matters. Training on automated systems takes time, so a returning pool of experienced seasonal workers is worth more at an automated site than at a manual one.

The bottom line

Automation is spreading through Phoenix distribution, but it is changing jobs more than eliminating them. The facilities that handle the shift well plan by task, invest in technical skills and keep a flexible, trained workforce for the work machines do not cover.

How EVs and Shifting Used-Car Volumes Affect Auction and Dealership Staffing

FLAT Staffing · October 30, 2026 · 4 min read

If you manage an auto auction or a dealership in the Valley, you already know your labor needs rise and fall with vehicle volume. What has changed in recent years is how unpredictable that volume has become, and how the mix of vehicles is shifting. Electric vehicles, lease cycles and supply swings in the used market all feed directly into how many drivers, porters, detailers and lot attendants you need on a given day.

This piece takes a qualitative look at those forces and what they mean for staffing.

Used-car supply moves in waves

Used vehicle supply follows new vehicle sales and leasing with a lag of several years. When new car production and leasing slowed earlier in the decade, it reduced the number of late-model vehicles returning to the market a few years later. When new sales and leasing recover, more vehicles eventually flow back through lease returns, fleet disposals and trade-ins.

For auctions, that means sale-day volume can swing noticeably from one season to the next, and sometimes from one week to the next. For dealerships, it affects how many trade-ins and auction purchases flow into reconditioning.

The staffing implication: your baseline crew should match your steady volume, and flexible labor should cover the swings. Carrying a full crew for peak volume year-round is expensive. Running lean and scrambling on heavy sale days hurts throughput and customer experience.

EVs change the work, not just the count

Electric vehicles are a growing share of what moves through Phoenix lots, and they bring some practical differences.

Charging and battery state

An EV that arrives with a low battery cannot simply be driven across the lot. Teams need procedures for checking charge, managing chargers and staging vehicles. That adds handling time and requires workers who understand the process.

Handling and safety training

EVs are often heavier than comparable gas vehicles, accelerate differently and can be very quiet at low speed. Lot drivers and porters benefit from specific orientation on EV handling, especially in crowded staging areas.

Condition reporting

Inspection and condition reports for EVs can include battery health information and other EV-specific items. Teams that write condition reports need to know what to capture.

Reconditioning

Detail and recon tasks are similar for EVs, but technicians need to know which components to avoid and which manufacturer procedures apply. Mechanical recon on EVs typically involves specially trained technicians.

Federal incentives changed in 2025

Federal tax policy is one of several factors that can affect EV demand. According to the IRS, the federal new and previously-owned clean vehicle credits are not available for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025. Shifts like that can influence buyer behavior, dealer inventory decisions and, eventually, what flows through auction lanes. We are not making predictions here, but it is the kind of change worth watching as you plan staffing mix.

Heat is a constant on Phoenix lots

Whatever the vehicle mix, auction and dealership lot work in Phoenix means long hours on hot pavement for much of the year. Arizona's heat safety guidance emphasizes water, rest, shade, training and acclimatization. Build those into staffing plans, especially for new or temporary drivers who have not yet adjusted to the conditions.

Staffing roles to plan for

Here are the roles we most often see flex with volume in the automotive space:

  • Lot drivers and porters who move vehicles between check-in, staging, lanes and pickup
  • Check-in and condition report staff who document vehicles on arrival
  • Detailers and recon helpers who prep vehicles for sale
  • Lane and sale-day support for auctions
  • Transport coordinators and yard attendants who keep inventory organized

Each of these benefits from a reliable core plus a trained flex pool that knows your site.

Practical steps for auction and dealership managers

  1. Track volume by day of week and by season. Use it to set a baseline crew and identify when you need flex labor.
  2. Train for EVs now. Add EV handling, charging procedures and safety to your standard orientation, including for temporary workers.
  3. Verify driver qualifications. Confirm license status and driving history requirements are met consistently for every driver, temp or direct.
  4. Plan for sale-day surges. Ask your staffing partner to keep a pool of workers already oriented to your lot so you are not training new people on your busiest day.
  5. Reassess quarterly. Vehicle mix and volume shift faster than they used to. Check your staffing model against actual volume every quarter.

The bottom line

Changing used-car supply and a growing share of EVs mean auction and dealership work is less predictable and more specialized than it used to be. Building a flexible, trained crew is the best way to handle both.

2026 Holiday Peak Season Outlook for Phoenix Distribution Centers

FLAT Staffing · October 28, 2026 · 4 min read

By the end of October, most Phoenix distribution centers have already made their big peak decisions. Headcount targets are set, shifts are drafted and the first seasonal workers are on the floor. But the next eight weeks still hold plenty of variables, and the operators who come out of December in good shape are usually the ones watching the right signals and adjusting early.

Rather than guess at a hiring number, here is how we read the current environment and what we would watch between now and New Year's.

The Phoenix industrial market keeps filling in

Metro Phoenix has spent several years adding large amounts of warehouse and distribution space, especially in the West Valley. That space is steadily being occupied. CBRE's Q3 2026 Phoenix industrial report put vacancy at 9.7 percent, down 150 basis points from a year earlier, with 1.59 million square feet of positive net absorption for the quarter.

For labor planning, the takeaway is simple: more occupied buildings means more operations competing for the same pool of pickers, packers, loaders and equipment operators, often within a few miles of each other along the same freeway corridors.

What shapes peak labor demand this year

We see a few forces worth tracking:

Retail and e-commerce volume

Holiday order volume drives fulfillment and parcel work more than any other factor. Watch your own customers' forecasts closely and ask them how confident they are. Volume that arrives later and more compressed than planned is harder to staff than volume that arrives early.

Large employers set the pace

When the biggest fulfillment and parcel operators in the Valley ramp up, they pull workers from everyone else. Starting pay, shift premiums and sign-on incentives at those sites shape what it takes for smaller operations to fill a shift. Keep an eye on what is being advertised along the I-10 and Loop 303 corridors.

The local labor market

The BLS reported the Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler metro unemployment rate at 4.9 percent (preliminary, not seasonally adjusted) for August 2026. That is a useful benchmark, but remember that warehouse labor is its own market. The real test is how many qualified people respond to your posting and actually show up for orientation.

January wage changes

Arizona's minimum wage is set to rise to $15.65 on January 1, 2027, based on the CPI formula in state law. If any seasonal workers will carry into January, build that into your bill rates and pay plans now.

How to use the next eight weeks

Plans made in August rarely survive November intact. Here is where we would focus:

  1. Lock in your forecast cadence. Agree with customers and your staffing partner on a weekly volume update. Small, frequent adjustments beat big last-minute scrambles.
  2. Stage a ready bench. Ask your agency to keep a group of screened, oriented workers available for surge days, rather than recruiting from scratch when volume spikes.
  3. Front-load training. Get forklift evaluations, safety orientation and site walkthroughs done before the busiest weeks, when trainers and leads are stretched thin.
  4. Watch week-one attendance. The first few days of a new hire's assignment tell you a lot. Address scheduling and transportation issues quickly, before they turn into turnover.
  5. Protect your core team. Long overtime stretches wear down your best people. Use seasonal labor to keep core staff productive through the final push.
  6. Plan the ramp-down. Decide in advance how and when you will release seasonal workers in January, and whether you want to keep top performers for returns season or convert them.

Returns season is part of peak

In fulfillment, December's outbound peak is followed by January's inbound returns. Many operations under-plan for this second wave. If you staff returns processing early, you can keep strong seasonal workers engaged instead of letting them walk away in late December.

A note on numbers

National seasonal hiring announcements get a lot of press every fall, but those figures rarely tell you much about a specific building in Tolleson or Goodyear. We would rather plan from your volume forecast, your historical attendance and what competing sites nearby are paying. Your own data beats a national headline.

The bottom line

Phoenix's industrial market continues to absorb space, which keeps competition for warehouse labor steady through the holidays. The best peak plans are flexible: a solid forecast cadence, a ready bench, early training and a clear plan for January.

Joint Employer Basics: What Changes When You Use a Staffing Agency

FLAT Staffing · October 26, 2026 · 4 min read

"Joint employer" is one of those phrases that makes operations managers nervous, usually because they have heard it in the context of a lawsuit. It does not need to be scary. Understanding the basic idea helps you use temporary labor confidently and keep the roles between you and your staffing partner clear.

This is a general overview. It is not legal advice, and the rules vary by law and by situation.

What joint employment means

In a staffing relationship, two companies have a hand in one worker's job:

  • The staffing agency recruits, hires, pays, withholds taxes, carries workers' comp and issues the W-2.
  • The client, or host employer, decides what work gets done and supervises it on site.

Joint employment is the idea that, depending on the facts, both companies can be considered employers of the same worker under certain laws. When that happens, both can share responsibility for compliance with those laws.

The important word is "certain." Different laws use different tests. The question is often asked separately for wage and hour law, labor relations law, workplace safety and anti-discrimination law.

Where the federal rules stand in 2026

The federal rules have changed several times over the past decade. Here is the current picture as of October 2026.

Labor relations (NLRB)

The National Labor Relations Board issued a broader joint employer rule in 2023, but a federal court vacated it in March 2024 before it took effect. In February 2026, the NLRB formally withdrew the 2023 rule and restored the text of its 2020 standard, which generally focuses on whether a company has substantial direct and immediate control over essential terms of employment such as wages, benefits, hours, hiring, discharge and supervision.

Wage and hour (DOL)

In April 2026, the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division proposed a new rule on joint employer status under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act. The comment period closed in June 2026. As of this writing, the proposal has not been finalized. If and when it is, the standard for wage and hour purposes could become more uniform nationwide.

Workplace safety (OSHA)

OSHA takes a practical view: staffing agencies and host employers share responsibility for temporary workers' safety. Each party is expected to address the hazards it is best positioned to control. That is less a legal test than an operating expectation.

What this means day to day

For most employers, the takeaway is not to avoid staffing agencies. It is to understand that how you manage temps on your floor matters, and to keep each party's role clear. A few areas to think about:

Supervision and direction

Directing the work is a normal part of using temporary labor. Your leads will assign tasks, set the pace and give feedback. That is expected.

Hiring, firing and discipline

These are areas where clear roles help. A common, sensible practice: the host tells the agency when a worker is not a fit for the assignment, and the agency handles the employment decision and any discipline. Avoid having your supervisors "fire" temps directly.

Pay and hours

The agency pays the worker. Make sure hours are recorded accurately and approved promptly, including any time spent in pre-shift meetings, security screening or required training. Unpaid off-the-clock time is a common source of wage claims, and in a joint employment scenario the host may share exposure.

Workplace conduct

Harassment and discrimination policies should apply to everyone on your floor. Make sure temps know how to report a concern, and make sure your supervisors know to pass reports to the agency right away.

Safety

Site-specific training, equipment and PPE are typically the host's job. General orientation and confirming the assignment is appropriate are typically the agency's. Put it in writing.

Questions to settle in your staffing agreement

  1. Who handles hiring, discipline and termination decisions?
  2. How are hours captured, approved and corrected?
  3. Who provides which training, and who supplies PPE?
  4. How are complaints and safety concerns reported and escalated?
  5. What are the insurance and indemnification terms? (Have counsel review these.)
  6. How does conversion to direct hire work?

A word on co-employment worries

Some employers worry that any involvement with a temp makes them the employer for every purpose. That is not how it works. The answers depend on the specific law and the actual facts. The best protection is a clear agreement, consistent practices and a staffing partner that handles its employer responsibilities well.

This article is general information only. For questions about your obligations, consult employment counsel or your HR advisor.

The bottom line

Joint employment is a legal concept, but it is managed through everyday habits: clear roles, accurate time records, consistent conduct policies and good communication with your agency. The federal rules are still evolving, so revisit your practices periodically.

If you want a partner that keeps the employer-side responsibilities clean, let's talk or call 602-730-3312.

Workers' Comp for Temp Workers: Who Covers What, the Agency or the Client?

FLAT Staffing · October 23, 2026 · 4 min read

One of the first questions a new client asks us is some version of: "If one of your people gets hurt at my facility, whose workers' comp pays?" It is a smart question. The answer is usually simple, but the details around it matter, and they are worth understanding before an incident, not after.

This is a general explainer, not legal advice. Workers' compensation law is state specific and fact specific.

The basics of workers' comp in Arizona

Arizona requires employers to secure workers' compensation coverage for their employees. Employers generally do this one of two ways:

  • Buying a policy from an insurance carrier authorized to write workers' comp in Arizona
  • Self-insuring, with approval and oversight from the Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA)

Workers' comp is a no-fault system. An injured employee receives medical and wage-replacement benefits regardless of who caused the injury. In exchange, an employer that has properly secured coverage is generally protected from being sued in tort by the employee for that injury. This trade-off is commonly called the exclusive remedy.

The ICA processes and adjudicates workers' comp claims in Arizona, and its Special Fund steps in for workers whose employers failed to carry coverage.

The typical arrangement with a staffing agency

In a standard temporary staffing relationship:

  • The staffing agency is the employer of record. It recruits, hires, pays and issues the W-2.
  • The agency carries the workers' compensation policy covering its employees, including those on assignment at your site.
  • The client (host employer) directs the day-to-day work and controls the physical workplace.

So in the normal case, when a temp is injured on assignment, the claim goes through the agency's workers' comp coverage. That is a big part of what you are paying for in the bill rate: the agency carries the payroll taxes, the comp premium and the claims administration.

Where it gets more nuanced

Workers' comp and liability questions around temporary workers can turn on specific facts. Courts in many states, including Arizona, have looked at concepts like "special employer" or "borrowed employee" status, which can treat a host employer as an employer of the temporary worker for certain purposes. Depending on the facts and the contract, that can affect questions like whether the host is also protected by the exclusive remedy, or whether the host could face a separate claim.

We are not going to try to summarize case law here. The practical takeaway is that the contract between you and your staffing agency, and the way the work is actually supervised, both matter. Have your counsel and your insurance broker review the arrangement.

Safety responsibility is shared

Separate from who pays a claim, there is the question of who is responsible for preventing injuries. OSHA's position is direct: staffing agencies and host employers are jointly responsible for maintaining a safe workplace for temporary workers. OSHA expects:

  • Host employers to treat temporary workers like any other workers on site, including training and hazard protection
  • Staffing agencies to inquire about and verify that the host has met its safety responsibilities
  • Both parties to clearly communicate and define responsibilities, ideally in their contract

In practice, the host is in the best position to provide site-specific training (equipment, layout, hazards), while the agency handles general safety orientation and confirms the assignment is appropriate.

What should be in your staffing agreement

A good agreement removes guesswork. Look for clear language on:

  1. Proof of coverage. Ask for a current certificate of insurance showing the agency's workers' comp and general liability coverage.
  2. Scope of work. Define the job duties temps will perform. If a temp is hired for picking and packing, you should not have them operate a forklift without the agency's knowledge and proper certification.
  3. Training responsibilities. Who provides general safety orientation and who provides site-specific and equipment training.
  4. PPE. Who supplies it, and which items.
  5. Injury reporting. How quickly the host notifies the agency, who arranges care, and who completes the required reports.
  6. Return to work. Whether the host can offer modified duty to an injured temp, which can help both the worker and claim costs.
  7. Indemnification and insurance terms. Have counsel review these.

Keeping claims down in the first place

The most expensive claim is the one that should not have happened. A few habits make a difference:

  • Match the person to the job. Assignments that involve lifting, heat or equipment need the right candidates.
  • Never change duties on the fly. Scope creep is a common source of temp injuries. If the work changes, tell the agency first.
  • Orient on day one. A 15-minute site walk covering exits, traffic lanes, dock edges and break areas prevents a lot of problems.
  • Report near misses. They are free lessons.
  • Report injuries promptly. Delays make claims harder for everyone, including the worker.

This article is general information, not legal or insurance advice. Consult your attorney and insurance broker about your specific arrangement.

The bottom line

In a typical staffing relationship, the agency employs the worker and carries their workers' comp. But the host controls the worksite, shares safety responsibility, and should have a clear written agreement covering coverage, duties and reporting.

Heat Illness Prevention in Arizona: What Warehouse and Outdoor Employers Need to Know

FLAT Staffing · October 21, 2026 · 4 min read

October brings some relief to the Valley, which makes it the right time to look back at the summer and plan for the next one. Heat illness prevention is no longer just a best practice in Arizona. Between new state guidelines, an active state emphasis program and a renewed federal enforcement push, employers with warehouse floors, auction lots, dealership lots and outdoor crews are being watched more closely than ever.

Here is where things stand as of fall 2026.

There is still no federal heat standard

Federal OSHA published a proposed heat injury and illness prevention rule in August 2024. The comment periods have closed, but the rule has not been finalized, and no final action date has been set.

That does not mean heat is unregulated. OSHA can and does cite employers for serious heat hazards under the General Duty Clause of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, which requires employers to keep workplaces free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm.

OSHA renewed its heat emphasis program in 2026

OSHA's National Emphasis Program on outdoor and indoor heat-related hazards first launched in 2022. In April 2026, OSHA issued an updated version (CPL 03-00-024) that runs for five more years. Key points from the update:

  • Heat priority days are days with a heat index of 80 degrees F or higher. On those days, inspectors on site for other reasons are expected to ask about the employer's heat program.
  • OSHA targets random heat inspections at establishments in designated high-hazard industries on days when the National Weather Service has issued a heat warning or advisory.
  • Inspectors are expected to look for heat hazards when there is evidence of them, such as injury logs, employee statements or what they can see on site.

What Arizona is doing

Arizona runs its own state OSHA plan through the Arizona Division of Occupational Safety and Health (ADOSH), part of the Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA).

The Heat Stress State Emphasis Program

ADOSH launched a Heat Stress State Emphasis Program in July 2023. Under it, inspectors focus on heat hazards during inspections where heat-related illness could occur, including programmed inspections on high-heat days in higher-risk industries. ADOSH has emphasized five core elements:

  • Adequate, cool drinking water
  • Rest breaks as needed
  • Shaded areas for recovery
  • Training on heat stress signs and symptoms
  • Acclimatization for new and returning workers

The 2026 Workplace Heat Safety Guidelines

In May 2025, Governor Hobbs signed an executive order creating a Workplace Heat Safety Task Force. The task force delivered its recommendations at the end of 2025, covering water, shade, rest, acclimatization, training and best practices for written Heat Illness Prevention Plans. On April 9, 2026, the Industrial Commission voted to approve and implement those recommendations, which feed into an updated emphasis program.

According to the ICA, these guidelines are not a new standard or rule. But employers can still be cited when heat conditions are not adequately addressed and are likely to cause death or serious harm. ADOSH also offers a downloadable heat plan template, which is a good starting point for smaller operations. Find it at azica.gov/heat.

Heat is not only an outdoor problem

Warehouse managers sometimes assume heat rules are about roofers and landscapers. In Phoenix, a dock door open to a 112-degree afternoon, a mezzanine with limited airflow or a trailer being unloaded in July can all create serious heat exposure. The same goes for auction lot drivers, porters and detail crews working on hot pavement.

A practical heat plan for 2027

Use the cooler months to get your program in writing. A solid plan typically covers:

  1. Water. Where it is, who keeps it stocked and how often workers are encouraged to drink.
  2. Rest and shade. Cool-down areas close to the work, and a culture where taking a break is expected, not frowned upon.
  3. Acclimatization. New and returning workers need time to build heat tolerance. Plan reduced exposure in their first days, especially early in the season.
  4. Training. Everyone, including supervisors and temps, should recognize heat exhaustion and heat stroke and know what to do.
  5. Monitoring. Track heat index and adjust work, such as moving heavy tasks to early shifts.
  6. Emergency response. Who calls 911, how to cool someone quickly and how to direct responders to your site.
  7. Records. Document training, incidents and plan reviews.

Temps and heat: shared responsibility

OSHA's position is that staffing agencies and host employers are jointly responsible for temporary workers' safety. In practice, the host controls the work environment, while the agency should confirm the host has proper protections in place and that its workers are trained.

Temps are also often the newest people on site, which means they are the least acclimatized. When you bring on a crew for a summer surge, acclimatization planning should apply to them from day one. We recommend agreeing in writing on who provides heat training, who supplies water and cooling, and how heat-related concerns are reported.

This is general information, not legal advice. Consult your safety professional or counsel about your specific obligations.

The bottom line

There is no single federal heat rule yet, but Arizona employers face active state and federal enforcement and clear expectations from ADOSH. A written plan, built now and practiced before May, protects your people and your operation.

If you want to coordinate heat planning for the temporary workers on your site, talk with our team or call 602-730-3312.

Arizona Earned Paid Sick Time (Prop 206): Basics for Employers Using Temps

FLAT Staffing · October 19, 2026 · 4 min read

Arizona voters approved Proposition 206, the Fair Wages and Healthy Families Act, in 2016. Along with the minimum wage increases most people remember, it created a statewide earned paid sick time requirement that took effect July 1, 2017. Nearly a decade later, we still field questions from operations and HR managers about how it works, especially when their workforce is a mix of direct employees and temps.

Here are the basics.

Who is covered

Arizona's earned paid sick time law applies to most private employers in the state, regardless of size. The Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA) enforces it, with rules in Title 20, Chapter 5, Article 12 of the Arizona Administrative Code. Full-time, part-time and temporary employees are all generally covered.

How accrual works

The core rules come from A.R.S. 23-372:

  • Accrual rate: Employees accrue at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked.
  • Annual cap, 15 or more employees: Employees are not entitled to accrue or use more than 40 hours per year, unless the employer sets a higher limit.
  • Annual cap, fewer than 15 employees: The cap is 24 hours per year, unless the employer sets a higher limit.
  • When accrual starts: At the start of employment.
  • Waiting period: An employer may require new employees to wait until the 90th calendar day of employment before using accrued time.
  • Carryover: Unused time carries over to the next year, subject to the annual use cap. Alternatively, an employer can pay out unused time at year end and front-load enough time at the start of the next year to meet the requirements.

The law defines a "year" as a regular and consecutive 12-month period determined by the employer, so your benefit year does not have to be the calendar year.

What employees can use it for

Arizona's law allows paid sick time for a broader set of reasons than many employers expect, including:

  • The employee's own illness, injury, health condition, medical care or preventive care
  • Care of a family member for the same reasons
  • Closure of the workplace or a child's school or place of care due to a public health emergency
  • Absences related to domestic violence, sexual violence, abuse or stalking

Employers may require reasonable documentation in some situations, and there are limits on what can be asked. Retaliation for using sick time is prohibited.

Where temps fit in

Here is where questions come up. When you bring in a worker through a staffing agency, the agency is typically the employer of record and handles accrual, tracking and payment of earned paid sick time for that worker. The hours a temp works on your site count toward their accrual with the agency, and when they use sick time, it comes through the agency's payroll.

A few points worth understanding:

Accrual follows the worker, not the assignment

A temp who moves from one client to another with the same agency generally keeps building time with that agency. If that worker shows up on your floor already past their 90th day with the agency, they may be eligible to use accrued time from their first day with you.

Absences still affect your schedule

Even though the agency pays the sick time, a protected absence still leaves a gap on your line. Ask your partner how they backfill when an assigned worker calls out for a covered reason. Sick time protections are one reason a deep bench matters more than a long roster.

Employer size can get complicated

The 24-hour versus 40-hour cap depends on employee count. For staffing agencies, which can have large numbers of workers across many clients, that count is typically well above 15. If your own company is near the threshold, how temps factor into your count is a question for your employment counsel, not a guess.

Temp-to-hire resets the relationship

When you convert a temp to your direct payroll, you become their employer for sick time purposes from that point. Talk with your HR advisor about how accrual and waiting periods apply to newly converted employees.

Practical steps for host employers

  1. Know your partner's policy. Ask how they track accrual, how workers request time, and how they notify you when a worker will be out.
  2. Build absence into staffing plans. If you need 40 people on the floor, plan for coverage when a few use sick time, especially during flu season, which overlaps with peak.
  3. Keep supervisors out of the eligibility question. Line leads should route absence questions to the agency and should never discourage a temp from using protected time.
  4. Review your own policy for direct employees. Make sure your handbook, payroll system and pay stubs meet the law's notice and recordkeeping requirements.
  5. Check local rules. Some cities have their own wage ordinances. If you operate outside the Phoenix metro, confirm whether additional rules apply.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Talk with your HR advisor or employment counsel about your specific situation.

The bottom line

Arizona's earned paid sick time law is not new, but it still trips up employers, particularly where temps and direct employees work side by side. The good news is that when you use a staffing agency, most of the administration sits with the agency. Your job is to plan for coverage and make sure supervisors handle absences correctly.

E-Verify in Arizona: Employer Requirements and How Staffing Agencies Handle I-9s

FLAT Staffing · October 16, 2026 · 5 min read

Arizona has one of the oldest and broadest E-Verify mandates in the country. If you hire people here, you are required to use it. But when part of your workforce comes through a staffing agency, a lot of managers are unsure where their responsibility ends and the agency's begins.

This piece walks through the basics: what Arizona requires, how Form I-9 and E-Verify fit together, and how verification works when you bring in temporary workers.

What Arizona law requires

Under the Legal Arizona Workers Act, all Arizona employers must use E-Verify for employees hired after December 31, 2007. That applies regardless of company size. Employers seeking state economic development incentives or government contracts face additional E-Verify requirements.

The enforcement teeth are real. According to the Arizona Attorney General's office, a county attorney can bring action to suspend or revoke the business licenses of an employer that knowingly or intentionally employs an unauthorized worker. Using E-Verify creates a rebuttable presumption that an employer did not knowingly hire an unauthorized worker, and good-faith compliance with the federal I-9 process can serve as an affirmative defense.

Form I-9 and E-Verify are two different things

People often use these terms interchangeably. They are not the same.

  • Form I-9 is the federal form every U.S. employer must complete for every new hire, documenting identity and work authorization. It is required nationwide.
  • E-Verify is the online system, run by the Department of Homeland Security with the Social Security Administration, that compares information from the I-9 against government records.

In practice, you complete the I-9 first, then create the E-Verify case using that information. The standard federal timing is that the employee completes Section 1 by the first day of work, and the employer completes Section 2 within three business days of the start date. Always use the current edition of the form posted by USCIS; editions do expire.

Who verifies a temp worker?

The short answer: the employer of record. When a staffing agency hires a worker, that agency is the one completing the I-9 and the E-Verify case.

E-Verify's own guidance for staffing agencies makes several points clear:

  • Staffing agencies must create E-Verify cases for all their new hires.
  • An agency cannot skip E-Verify because a client asks it to.
  • An agency must not verify selectively, such as only for certain clients or certain workers. Verification has to be applied consistently.
  • Agencies can set the employee's first day of employment either as the date the person is first assigned to a job or the date they accept an offer and enter the assignment pool, as long as they use that approach consistently. They should not leave the certification date or first day of employment blank.

For host employers, E-Verify's guidance is that you should confirm with your staffing agency that it has verified the workers it places with you. An agency can show proof of its enrollment by printing its E-Verify company information page.

What host employers should ask

You do not complete I-9s for agency employees, but you should not take compliance on faith either. Here is what we would ask any staffing partner, including us:

  1. Are you enrolled in E-Verify, and can you show proof?
  2. Do you verify every new hire, not just those going to certain clients?
  3. When do you complete the I-9 and create the E-Verify case relative to the first assignment?
  4. How do you handle a tentative nonconfirmation? The process has specific steps and notice requirements for the employee. Your partner should know them cold.
  5. Do you complete I-9s in person or use the DHS alternative procedure for remote document review? The remote option is available only to employers enrolled in E-Verify and in good standing, and it comes with its own rules.
  6. How do you store and retain I-9 records, and could you produce them in an audit?
  7. What happens if you convert a temp to your direct employee? When you hire someone directly, you become the employer and need to complete your own I-9 and E-Verify case. The agency's paperwork does not transfer to you.

Common mistakes we see

A few patterns cause trouble for employers, with or without agencies:

  • Treating E-Verify as optional for small teams. In Arizona, it is not.
  • Running E-Verify before a job offer. E-Verify is for new hires, not applicant screening.
  • Asking for specific documents. Employees choose which acceptable documents to present from the lists on the form. Requesting particular documents can create discrimination exposure.
  • Skipping re-verification tracking. Some work authorizations expire. Employers need a system for tracking those dates without over-documenting.
  • Assuming a temp-to-hire carries over. It does not. New employer, new I-9.

Why this matters for operations, not just HR

When verification goes wrong, the problems often show up on the floor first: a worker can't start on time, a crew comes up short on day one, or a large group has to be re-processed. A staffing partner with tight onboarding moves verification ahead of the start date so your shift is not waiting on paperwork.

This is general information, not legal advice. For questions about your specific obligations, consult employment or immigration counsel.

The bottom line

Arizona expects every employer to verify every new hire. When you use a staffing agency, that job belongs to the agency as employer of record, but you should still confirm they are doing it consistently and correctly.

Arizona Minimum Wage 2027: What the Expected Increase Means for Labor Budgets

FLAT Staffing · October 14, 2026 · 5 min read

Every fall, Arizona employers get the same piece of news: the state minimum wage is going up in January. For 2027, the formula in state law points to about $15.65 per hour, up 50 cents from the current $15.15 (the Industrial Commission of Arizona publishes the official rate each fall, so confirm it once posted). That is not a headline-grabbing jump, but if you run a warehouse, an auction lane or a dealership service drive with a lot of hourly people, those 50 cents ripple through your budget in ways that are easy to underestimate.

Here is how the rate is set, what is confirmed, and how we suggest Phoenix-area operations leaders plan for it.

How Arizona sets the minimum wage

Arizona's minimum wage is tied to inflation by state law. Under A.R.S. 23-363, the rate is adjusted every January 1 by the increase in the federal Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers (CPI-U, U.S. city average), measured from August of one year to August of the next. The increase is rounded to the nearest five cents.

That means the new number is effectively locked in once the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the August CPI report each September. The Industrial Commission of Arizona (ICA), which enforces the minimum wage law, then posts the official notice and updated poster. Last year the ICA published its 2026 notice on October 2.

The 2027 math

The BLS reported on September 11, 2026 that CPI-U rose 3.4 percent in the 12 months ending August 2026. Apply that to the current rate:

  • 2026 rate: $15.15
  • 3.4 percent increase: about 51.5 cents
  • Rounded to the nearest nickel: 50 cents
  • Expected 2027 rate: about $15.65, effective January 1, 2027 (pending the official ICA notice)

The law also lets employers pay tipped employees up to $3.00 less per hour than the minimum, as long as wages plus tips meet the full minimum for every hour worked. For most of the industries we staff, tip credits do not apply, but it is worth knowing.

A note on local rates: Flagstaff and Tucson set their own, higher minimums. If you run crews outside the Phoenix metro, check those cities separately.

As of this writing, the ICA had not yet posted its formal 2027 notice. Watch the ICA minimum wage page for the official poster and confirm before you finalize payroll settings.

Why a 50-cent raise costs more than 50 cents

If you only have a handful of people at the minimum, the direct cost is small. The real impact comes from three places.

1. Wage compression

Most warehouse and yard jobs in the Valley already pay above the state minimum. But when the floor rises, the gap between your entry-level rate and your experienced or lead rates shrinks. A forklift operator who earned $3 more than a new picker now earns $2.50 more. People notice. Many employers end up moving several pay bands, not just the bottom one.

2. Payroll burden

Every dollar of wages carries employer-side costs: payroll taxes, workers' compensation premiums (often calculated on payroll) and in some cases benefits tied to earnings. When you model the increase, model the fully loaded cost, not the hourly rate alone.

3. Overtime

Overtime is paid at one-and-a-half times the regular rate. If your peak weeks run heavy on overtime, a higher base rate raises that cost too.

How to budget for 2027

Here is the approach we recommend to operations and HR leaders building next year's labor plan:

  1. Pull a rate census. List every hourly role, its current rate and headcount. Flag anyone under $15.65 and anyone within roughly a dollar of it.
  2. Decide your compression policy. Will you move only the people below the new floor, or adjust bands above it? Make the call deliberately rather than reacting when someone quits.
  3. Recalculate loaded cost per hour. Include payroll taxes and comp. This is the number that belongs in your budget, not the posted wage.
  4. Revisit your staffing bill rates. If you use a staffing partner, bill rates for roles near the minimum will move on January 1. Ask your agency for updated rates now so the change does not surprise your finance team.
  5. Update postings and systems. New posters, offer letters, job ads and timekeeping rules should all reflect the new rate before the first payroll of 2027.
  6. Look at the competitive rate, not just the legal one. In practice, the rate that fills shifts in Phoenix distribution is often set by what the large employers down the road are paying. The legal minimum is a floor, not a recruiting strategy.

What this means if you use temporary labor

When you use a staffing agency, the agency is the employer of record and is responsible for paying at least the legal minimum. But the cost lands on you through the bill rate. A good partner will tell you ahead of time which assignments are affected and by how much.

We also suggest using the increase as a moment to check whether your temp pay rates are competitive enough to keep people showing up. A rate that was attractive in early 2026 may look ordinary once the new floor kicks in.

This article is general information, not legal or tax advice. Confirm specific obligations with your HR advisor or employment counsel.

The bottom line

The 2027 increase is modest, predictable and already calculable. The employers who handle it well are the ones who build it into their Q4 budget instead of discovering it in January payroll.
